title: Effect of percutaneous electrolysis combined with exercise on pain and function in chronic lateral epicondylitis: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Percutaneous electrolysis (PE) is a minimally invasive, ultrasound-guided treatment, but its added benefit alongside exercise for chronic lateral epicondylitis remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To compare exercise plus PE with exercise alone for pain and function.
DESIGN: Prospective randomized controlled trial.
METHODS: In an outpatient rehabilitation clinic, 68 participants were randomized to exercise plus PE (n = 34) or exercise alone (n = 34). Both groups performed a 2-week home-based stretching and strengthening program; PE was administered on days 1, 8, and 14. The primary outcome was pain intensity on a 0-10 visual analog scale (VAS); secondary outcomes were Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE) total score, pressure pain threshold (PPT), and Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (Q-DASH) score. Assessments occurred at baseline and 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months after treatment completion.
RESULTS: Group-by-time interactions were significant for all outcomes (all p < 0.001). At 3 months, model-estimated between-group mean differences favored PE for VAS (-3.30 points; 95% CI, -3.97 to -2.63) and PRTEE (-20.78 points; 95% CI, -25.98 to -15.57), both p < 0.001. Secondary outcomes favored PE at all follow-ups. In a post hoc exploratory responder analysis, clinically meaningful PRTEE improvement occurred in 79.4% of the PE group versus 2.9% of controls (p < 0.001). No serious adverse events or intervention-related discontinuations occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: Adding ultrasound-guided PE to the tested 2-week home exercise program was associated with greater improvements in pain and function than exercise alone over the 3-month follow-up. Longer-term effects and applicability to other rehabilitation programs remain uncertain.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07277127.

title: Management of Hand Injuries: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Surgical and Rehabilitation Strategies.
abstract: Management of traumatic hand injuries has evolved substantially with advances in anesthesia, tendon repair, biological adjuncts, fracture fixation, and rehabilitation. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary evidence on surgical and rehabilitation strategies for improving functional recovery and reducing complications after acute hand trauma. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261320700). PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for studies published from January 2000 to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials and prospective comparative studies evaluating contemporary strategies for flexor or extensor tendon injuries and metacarpal or phalangeal fractures were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Of 3417 records identified, 354 duplicates were removed and 3063 records were screened. Following full-text assessment, 23 studies were included. Evidence supported the use of wide-awake local anesthesia no tourniquet (WALANT) as a safe alternative to general anesthesia, although functional superiority was not consistent across trials. Acellular dermal matrices, biological amnion, hydrogels, hyaluronic acid, and other adjuncts showed potential for reducing adhesions and improving tendon gliding. Early active mobilization and place-and-hold protocols produced favorable functional outcomes, while relative motion extension orthoses improved early function after extensor tendon repair. Smartphone-assisted rehabilitation improved adherence. Headless compression screws facilitated earlier functional recovery in selected metacarpal fractures, while multistrand tendon repairs provided sufficient strength for early mobilization. Contemporary hand injury management increasingly integrates WALANT, robust tendon repair, anti-adhesion adjuncts, early active rehabilitation, modern orthoses, and digital adherence tools. However, heterogeneity and variable risk of bias across studies warrant cautious interpretation and further high-quality comparative research.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.
METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

title: Platelet-Rich Plasma versus Corticosteroid Injections for Subacromial Impingement Syndrome: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Subacromial impingement syndrome (SAI) is a common cause of shoulder pain. Corticosteroid injection (CS) provides short-term relief, but concerns about tendon health and durability have increased interest in platelet-rich plasma (PRP) as an alternative. This meta-analysis compared pain and functional outcomes after PRP versus CS for SAI.
METHODS: A systematic review was performed per PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials comparing PRP and CS for SAI. VAS pain scores and shoulder-specific functional outcomes were extracted, and random-effects meta-analyses were performed at baseline, short-term, and mid-term follow-up.
RESULTS: Eight studies (518 patients; 7 RCTs and 1 non-randomized comparative study) were included, with 259 patients per group. Baseline VAS scores were comparable (MD 0.03, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.15; I2 = 0%). Short- and mid-term VAS scores showed no significant difference between groups (short-term MD 0.47, 95% CI -0.35 to 1.29; mid-term MD 0.50, 95% CI -1.80 to 2.80), though heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 93.6% and 98.0%), falling to 49.2% and 80.2% after excluding the non-randomized study. Functional outcomes were inconsistently reported; at 6 months, Constant score differences ranged from -13.0 to +17.2, and UCLA differences ranged from -0.6 to +0.3.
CONCLUSION: PRP and CS showed no significant difference in short- or mid-term pain relief for SAI, but heterogeneity between trials was substantial. Functional outcomes were inconsistently reported across studies. Current evidence does not show it is clinically superior to CS for pain relief, and treatment choice should still weigh cost, availability, and patient preference.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, Systematic Review.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups.
METHODS: Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups.
RESULTS: A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Female Team-Sport Athletes' Physical Fitness and Jump Performance Kinematics After Plyometric Jump Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plyometric jump training (PJT) can improve athletes' physical fitness across a range of sports and populations. Nonetheless, the role of PJT in adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics remains unclear, particularly given the increasing number of published, heterogeneous studies.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to first examine the effectiveness of PJT in improving physical fitness and jump-performance kinematics in adult female team-sport athletes, and second, to provide evidence-based recommendations for PJT prescription for this population.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO databases up to March 2026. The included studies recruited healthy female team-sport athletes (mean age: ≥ 18 years), incorporated a PJT programme ≥ 2 weeks in duration, included comparator groups, and assessed athletes' physical fitness, jump performance, and/or kinematics. The risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Hedges' g effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were reported using a random-effects model for meta-analyses. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the participant characteristics (height, body mass, sport) and PJT programming variables (duration, frequency, total sessions, weekly total jumps). The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Thirty-one articles were included (n = 609 participants), and 25 were meta-analysed. Two studies were categorised with high RoB (≤ 3 points), 20 studies achieved moderate RoB (4-5 points), and 9 studies achieved low RoB (≥ 6 points). Compared to controls, PJT improved countermovement jump (CMJ) height (ES = 0.550, p < 0.001), CMJ peak concentric velocity (ES = 0.623, p = 0.011), drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) (ES = 0.926, p = 0.001), DJ height (ES = 0.721, p = 0.002), 10 m sprint time (ES = 0.712, p = 0.032), 20 m sprint time (ES = 0.709, p < 0.001), 30 m sprint time (ES = 1.018, p = 0.001), non-linear (agility) Illinois test time (ES = 1.225, p < 0.001) and T test sprint time (ES = 0.965, p < 0.001). Compared to PJT ≤ 6 weeks, longer interventions favoured DJ RSI (p = 0.008), 10 m sprint time (p = 0.001), and Illinois agility test time (p < 0.001). Impact of heterogeneity (I2) remained low (≤ 0.06%) in five analyses and moderate in the other four analyses (≤ 73.1%). The certainty of evidence was considered low to moderate for the study outcomes. Two studies reported that a total of three participants possibly sustained an injury during PJT.
CONCLUSIONS: Adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics improved after PJT when compared to the control condition, including CMJ height, CMJ peak concentric velocity, DJ RSI, linear sprint speed, and non-linear (agility) sprint speed. The improvements were particularly notable with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks).
TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NERCY.

title: Web-based rehabilitation after surgical salvage procedures for wrist osteoarthritis: protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Wrist osteoarthritis (OA) is a disabling condition often affecting individuals of working age and frequently resulting from previous trauma. When non-operative management fails, surgical salvage procedures may reduce pain but require structured postoperative rehabilitation. Telerehabilitation has demonstrated comparable outcomes to standard face-to-face rehabilitation in several musculoskeletal conditions; however, evidence following its effectiveness after wrist OA surgery is lacking. This trial aims to evaluate whether a web-based rehabilitation programme is non-inferior to standard, face-to-face rehabilitation following surgical salvage procedures for wrist OA.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a prospective, parallel-group, assessor-blinded, randomised controlled non-inferiority trial conducted at a tertiary hand surgery centre. 90 adults undergoing surgical salvage procedures for wrist OA (four-corner fusion, lunocapitate fusion, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid fusion, radioscapholunate fusion or proximal row carpectomy) will be randomised 1:1 to receive either postoperative web-based rehabilitation or standard face-to-face rehabilitation. The primary outcome is the patient-rated wrist evaluation score measured 12 weeks after immobilisation has ended. Secondary outcomes include pain, health-related quality of life, fear of movement, range of motion, grip strength, patient-reported experience, adherence and cost of rehabilitation.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval has been granted by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority in November 2024. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT06814821

title: Application of antibiotic-loaded bone cement in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: inhibiting IL-6 levels and reducing postoperative infection rate.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We aim to clarify the inhibitory effect of antibiotic-loaded bone cement (ALBC) on inflammatory factors, and its preventive effect on postoperative infections in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA).
METHODS: This prospective randomized controlled trial enrolled 104 osteoarthritis patients undergoing UKA, randomly assigned to the non-ALBC group (n = 52, bone cement without antibiotics) and ALBC group (ALBC with 1.0 g vancomycin hydrochloride, n = 52). Primary outcomes were postoperative inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, TNF-α, IL-6); secondary outcomes included infection rate and HSS score. Independent-samples t-tests were used for continuous variables, χ2 test for categorical variables (infection rate, efficacy), and repeated measures analysis of variance for intra-group longitudinal comparisons.
RESULTS: The ALBC group demonstrated lower inflammatory markers at postoperative day 7 and at 3 months [CRP (3.52 ± 0.81 vs 6.92 ± 1.17, Cohen's d = 3.379), ESR (16.29 ± 2.31 vs 20.19 ± 4.05, Cohen's d = 1.183), TNF-α (29.71 ± 4.03 vs 36.25 ± 5.17, Cohen's d = 1.411), and IL-6 (17.05 ± 3.72 vs 22.05 ± 4.38, Cohen's d = 1.230)] (all p < 0.001), and also showed superior clinical outcomes, with lower postoperative infection rate (p = 0.016), higher HSS score (p < 0.001), and better overall clinical efficacy (p = 0.010) than the non-ALBC group.
CONCLUSION: The application of ALBC in UKA was associated with reduced postoperative inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and a lower incidence of postoperative infection. These findings suggest that ALBC may play a beneficial role in postoperative recovery and joint function rehabilitation.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA.
METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year.
RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA.

title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

title: Multi-planar patellar hypomobility as a potential contributor to VMO-VL dyssynergy and return to sport limitations following ACL reconstruction in soccer players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patellofemoral hypomobility (PFH) is a frequent yet underestimated complication following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. PFH induces biomechanical and neuromuscular alterations that impair return to sport (RTS) and accelerate early joint degeneration. However, current evidence describes PFH primarily as an associated factor rather than a direct causal determinant of RTS failure. Therefore, the primary objective of this review is to analyze the correlation between PFH and functional complications during RTS. The study also aims to summarize the available evidence on the relationship between PFH and medium- to long-term clinical outcomes, without implying causal predictions where not supported.
METHODS: A narrative review was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science using a Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO)-structured search. No systematic review procedures or pooled quantitative analyses were performed; all numerical data derived from individual studies. Included studies involved athletes aged 18-35 undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BPTB) or Hamstring autografts.
RESULTS: The analysis reveals significant PFH (>25% compared to the contralateral side) in 15-22% of athletes at 6 months, with a peak of 28% in BPTB graft cases. Longitudinal hypomobility correlates with extension deficit, whereas transverse hypomobility is associated with increased anterior knee pain (AKP) in 34% of cases. Data indicate a 12-15% reduction in Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance and a 3.4-fold higher risk of patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) within 5 years, although PFH was not directly measured as an independent variable in these studies. Additionally, 25% of athletes with PFH discontinue competitive activity within 36 months after RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: PFH emerges as an important factor associated with postoperative functional limitations. Restricted patellar glide disrupts the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)/vastus lateralis (VL) synergy, reduces performance, and accelerates cartilage degeneration. Symmetry of patellar kinematics should be considered a relevant parameter for RTS decision-making, while acknowledging that RTS outcomes are multifactorial and not solely determined by PFH.

title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) causes pain and functional limitation. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is increasingly used as a supportive treatment. Optimal rehabilitation after PRP is unclear. This study investigated the effectiveness of a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach on pain and function.
METHODS: Sixty participants with SAPS were randomized to two groups; 54 completed the study and were included in the final per-protocol analysis (27 per group). During a 21-day period, the study group received a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach in addition to standard conventional physiotherapy, while the control group received standard conventional physiotherapy alone. Range of motion, muscle strength, and posture were evaluated. In addition, outcome measures included the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), Functional Impairment Test-Hand and Neck/Shoulder/Arm (FIT-HaNSA) and Constant-Murley Shoulder Score, which were administered for assessment purposes.
RESULTS: Corbin Posture Scale scores decreased in both groups (p < 0.05). Pain reduction was greater in the study group (VAS: from 9.00 ± 0.67 to 2.92 ± 1.14 versus from 9.11 ± 0.64 to 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: from 27.07 ± 4.41 to 10.07 ± 3.33 versus from 21.33 ± 2.46 to 19.37 ± 2.35; p < 0.001). Improvements in Constant-Murley, DASH, and FIT-HaNSA scores, shoulder muscle strength, and active and passive range of motion were significantly greater in the study group (p < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to standard conventional physiotherapy may provide additional short-term improvements in pain, muscle strength, range of motion, and shoulder function compared with standard conventional physiotherapy alone in individuals with SAPS. However, long-term follow-up was not conducted. Therefore, the sustainability of the observed improvements remains unclear. Future studies should investigate the long-term effects of structured post-PRP rehabilitation approaches.

title: Return-to-Play Outcomes After Primary Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Vary Substantially Depending on Return Criteria: A Systematic Review Stratified by Competition Level.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine how return definitions influence return to play (RTP), return to the same level of play (RTSP), advancement rates, and return timelines after primary ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (UCLR) in baseball pitchers across levels of competition.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from January 2000 to January 2025. Studies evaluating baseball pitchers undergoing primary UCLR and reporting RTP, RTSP, advancement, or return timing outcomes with participation-based (RTP based on a single event) or durability-based (RTP after sustained participation over a predefined threshold) criteria were included. Primary outcomes were RTP, RTSP, and advancement rate (progression to a higher level after UCLR); secondary outcome was return time stratified by return criteria. Risk of bias was assessed with the Methodological Index for Non-randomized Studies and Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tools.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies met inclusion. Across these studies, 19 included Major League Baseball players (2194 players), 5 included Minor League Baseball (MiLB) players (2318 players), 4 included collegiate athletes (553 athletes), and 6 included high school athletes (258 athletes). RTP/RTSP rates were 86% to 92%/70% to 87% in high school, 84%/67% to 92% in college, 76.3% to 79%/69.1% to 100% in MiLB, and 80% to 97.2%/28.1% to 87% in Major League Baseball. Advancement was 55.7% to 63.2% in high school, 4.1% to 44.4% in college, and 22.3% to 45% in MiLB. Surgery-to-return time using the common RTSP definition ranged from 13.7 to 20.5 months (Major League Baseball), 14.6 to 16.4 (MiLB), and 11 to 17 (college and high school). Durability-based definitions were not consistently associated with longer return intervals.
CONCLUSIONS: Without standardized return criteria, reported RTP, RTSP, advancement rates, and return timelines after primary UCLR in baseball pitchers varied substantially across studies and competition levels. Durability-based criteria were not consistently associated with longer return timelines, indicating that return outcomes should be interpreted according to the competition level and return definition used. Standardized, tier-specific return criteria may improve clinical interpretation after primary UCLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV studies.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Zone I Flexor Digitorum Profundus Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Last 25 Years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Zone I flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon injuries, at the distal phalanx insertion, generally require surgery. However, outcomes may vary, and multiple surgical techniques have been described. This review sought to evaluate management, rehabilitation, and outcomes following zone I FDP injuries.
METHODS: Using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, a systematic review and meta-analysis was performed. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane were queried for articles concerning zone I FDP injuries since 2000. Patients younger than 18 years of age and revision surgery were excluded. Demographics, strength, range of motion, outcome scores, therapy protocols, and complications were evaluated.
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria and were stratified by treatment strategy into 31 cohorts comprising 669 fingers. The mean age was 36 years and 25% were women. Injury mechanisms included 348 lacerations (52%) and 234 avulsions (35%); 88 injuries (13%) were unspecified. Primary tenorrhaphy was the most frequently reported treatment (39%), followed by tenorrhaphy with a tie-over button (10%) and bone anchor fixation (10%). The mean time to surgery was 4 days. Range of motion or outcome measures were documented in 12 cohorts (39%) and strength in 10 cohorts (32%). Meta-analysis demonstrated postoperative FDP rupture, revision surgery, and tenolysis rates of 2.0%, 1.0%, and 1.6%, respectively. Lacerations were treated with primary tenorrhaphy more commonly compared with avulsions (59% vs 22%) and had higher revision rates (7.6% vs 1.4%).
CONCLUSIONS: Surgical repair of zone I FDP injuries demonstrates low complication rates and generally favorable outcomes; however, inconsistent reporting of functional outcomes limits meaningful comparison between surgical techniques.

title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing.
STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5.
RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Outcomes of open and endoscopic excision of a symptomatic os trigonum in athletes: a systematic review with exploratory analysis of prognostic factors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A symptomatic os trigonum causes posterior ankle impingement in athletes and is excised when conservative treatment fails. Previous syntheses have pooled mean outcomes across mixed populations, and poor outcomes have not been defined consistently.
METHODS: Six databases were searched for open or endoscopic os trigonum excision in athletes, following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM. Techniques were compared within comparative studies, with supplementary pooling. A composite poor-outcome profile and eight candidate factors were examined at study-arm level.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies (17 arms, 440 participants) were included. Failure to return to prior level was uncommon (9 of 438; 0-6.2% by arm). In the randomised trial, return to prior sport level was 4.4 weeks faster after endoscopic excision (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.7-6.1); pooling two further non-randomised studies with imputed SDs gave 4.9 weeks (95% CI 3.3-6.6). Trial complications occurred in 1 of 26 endoscopic and 6 of 26 open patients (odds ratio 7.50, 95% CI 0.83-67.49); the two-study pooled odds ratio was 5.59 (95% CI 1.10-28.35) from 10 events. Both nerve injuries described as permanent followed open surgery. The composite depended on arm size and threshold choice, and five of eight candidate factors could not be tested.
CONCLUSION: Poor outcomes are uncommon after either approach. Low-certainty evidence suggests faster return to sport after endoscopic excision; complication evidence is of very low certainty, though no nerve injury described as permanent followed endoscopic excision. A consensus definition of return to sport is needed.

title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.
METHODS: In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.
RESULTS: EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: -10.9%, 95%CI: -21.4;-0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: -9.80, 95%CI: -18.3;-1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.
CONCLUSION: n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.

title: Effects of Exercise Type and Duration on Pain, Function, and Quality of Life in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review With Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the effects of aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, and combined interventions on pain, function, and quality of life (QoL) in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA) at the short term (≤12 weeks) and long term (>12 weeks). DESIGN: Intervention systematic review with Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA). LITERATURE SEARCH: MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PEDro, AMED, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception until July 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials of patients with knee OA that evaluated exercise interventions aimed at improving pain, function, and QoL. DATA SYNTHESIS: Using random-effects models, the NMA synthesized effect sizes and ranked interventions by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), with evidence certainty assessed via the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. RESULTS: Thirty-five trials (n = 3808 patients) were included. For pain, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect among the interventions (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.937, low certainty). For function, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect estimates (SMD = -0.590, low certainty), followed by long-term aerobic exercise (SMD = -0.540, very low certainty). Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect (SMD = 0.663, low certainty) for improving QoL. CONCLUSION: Aerobic and resistance exercise, alone or in combination, and delivered over the short- or long-term, improved pain, function, and QoL for patients with knee OA. Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had clinically meaningful improvements for pain, with relatively favorable effects on function and QoL. Evidence regarding the clinical significance of long-term exercise interventions was limited. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(11):724-734. Epub 24 July 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.13875.

title: First-Hand Experience and the Value of Telerehabilitation for Chronic Knee Pain: A Discrete Choice Experiment Nested in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess whether first-hand experience of receiving physical therapy via telerehabilitation affected patient preferences and willingness to pay for telerehabilitation. DESIGN: This study used a discrete choice experiment nested within a randomized controlled trial. METHODS: We recruited 319 Australian adults aged 45 years or over, with chronic knee pain consistent with osteoarthritis, who had completed a clinical trial where they were randomized to receive physical therapy via telerehabilitation or in-person. Participants were presented hypothetical scenarios and asked to choose between physical therapy delivered via telerehabilitation or in-person. Each scenario presented seven attributes of consultations at varying levels. Data were analyzed using a generalized multinomial logit and latent class models. RESULTS: There were 164 participants from the in-person trial arm (80% of those randomized) and 155 from the telerehabilitation arm (82% of those randomized) who participated. Participants in the telerehabilitation arm (ie, with first-hand experience of telerehabilitation) were willing to pay AU$ 87.49 (95% confidence interval: 72.83, 102.14) more than people in the in-person arm for telerehabilitation consultations (all other attributes fixed at reference values for categorical variables and at mean values for continuous variables). Four subgroups were identified. In the telerehabilitation arm, 105 (68% of 155) participants preferred telerehabilitation, and 50 (32%) preferred in-person consultations. In the in-person arm, 63 (39% of 164) held a strong preference for in-person consultations, and 101 (61%) had a mild preference for in-person consultations. CONCLUSION: People with first-hand experience using telerehabilitation for physical therapy expressed a greater willingness to use and pay for it than people who experienced in-person care. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(11):735-744. Epub 23 September 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14073.

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.
METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.
RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.
CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on vitamin D status and physical performance in football players: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Low vitamin D status is frequently reported among athletes, but whether vitamin D supplementation improves physical performance in football players remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration, jump performance, sprint performance, aerobic capacity, and muscular performance in association football and futsal players.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026. Controlled intervention studies comparing vitamin D supplementation with control conditions were eligible. Standardized mean differences were calculated as Hedges' g and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261430873).
RESULTS: Eleven reports representing nine independent studies and 312 players were included. In RCT-only primary analyses, vitamin D supplementation was associated with higher circulating 25(OH)D concentrations (g = 1.41, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.92; I² = 58.0%). Pooled effects were not statistically significant for jump performance (g = 0.21, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.53), sprint performance (g = -0.03, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.34), aerobic capacity (g = 0.00, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.45), or muscular performance (g = 0.19, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.51). The certainty of evidence was low for circulating 25(OH)D, jump performance, and muscular performance, and very low for sprint performance and aerobic capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: Vitamin D supplementation was associated with increased circulating 25(OH)D concentrations, whereas current evidence is insufficient to support a consistent improvement in physical performance. Given the low to very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials using standardized, football-relevant performance tests are warranted.

title: A Study of Functional Outcome of Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Hamstring Graft.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is a common cause of knee instability and functional limitation. Arthroscopic reconstruction using hamstring tendon autografts is widely used because of favorable functional outcomes and lower donor-site morbidity.
AIM: This study aims to evaluate the clinical and functional outcomes of patients undergoing arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using a hamstring tendon autograft.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of Orthopaedics, M.G.M. Medical College and L.S.K. Hospital, Kishanganj, Bihar. Fifty patients aged 18-50 years with clinically and radiologically confirmed ACL tears underwent primary arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using a quadrupled hamstring tendon autograft. Femoral fixation was performed using a cortical button and tibial fixation using an interference screw. Patients were followed at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months. Functional outcome was assessed using the Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale, while clinical stability and post-operative complications were documented. No comparator group was included. The study was confined to one institution, and no instrumented laxity measurements or formal return-to-sport outcomes were reported.
RESULTS: The mean age of participants was 31.72 ± 8.88 years, and 72% were male. Road traffic accidents were the commonest mechanism of injury (44%), followed by sports-related injuries (36%). Medial meniscal tear was the most common associated injury (40%). Fifteen of 50 patients (30%) experienced a recorded post-operative complication. In the total cohort, anterior knee pain occurred in 5/50 (10%), tunnel widening in 4/50 (8%), infection in 3/50 (6%), and tibial screw dislodgement, graft failure, and knee stiffness in 1/50 (2%) each. The mean Lysholm score improved from 50.74 ± 6.342 preoperatively to 86.00 ± 10.067 postoperatively (P < 0.05); 52% had good, and 32% had excellent Lysholm outcomes at final follow-up.
CONCLUSION: In this single-center prospective observational cohort of 50 patients, Lysholm scores improved over 12 months after hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction, with 84% classified as having good-to-excellent outcomes. These findings describe short-term recovery within the treated cohort. The absence of a comparator and adjusted analyses precludes causal attribution or conclusions about superiority over alternative reconstruction strategies or non-operative management; long-term effectiveness and return to sport were not established.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Post-Treatment Follow-up, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport: Proceedings of the International Consensus Meetings on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle.
abstract: BackgroundPostoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and return to sport (RTS) are key components of recovery following surgical management of osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT). However, substantial variability exists in postoperative protocols, with limited high-quality evidence guiding clinical practicesMethodsInternational experts convened during the International Congress on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA) in Pittsburgh, USA (2017), with subsequent ratification of recommendations in New York, USA (2025). The original consensus statements were developed using a modified Delphi process involving electronic surveys, structured questionnaires, and expert discussion. Consensus strength was defined as consensus (51%-74%), strong consensus (75%-99%), or unanimous (100%). The recommendations addressed postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following OLT management.ResultsA total of 16 consensus statements were developed and subsequently ratified, comprising 7 statements addressing post-treatment follow-up and 9 addressing rehabilitation and RTS. All statements achieved strong consensus, with agreement ranging from 75% to 98%. Follow-up recommendations emphasized standardized clinical assessment and patient-reported outcomes, with extended monitoring in select patients. Rehabilitation recommendations supported early controlled motion and progressive weightbearing, with individualized progression according to procedure and clinical performance. Return to sport recommendations emphasized functional recovery and individualized decision-making. Ten statements (63%) were classified exclusively as Grade E, highlighting the limited evidence supporting several recommendations.ConclusionThe ICCRA consensus statements establish a structured framework for postoperative follow-up, rehabilitation, and RTS following surgical management of OLT. Despite strong expert agreement, several recommendations remain supported by limited evidence, underlining the need for prospective studies to establish validated, procedure-specific rehabilitation protocols and objective RTS criteria.Level of Evidence:V, expert consensus.

title: Sex-Equitable Machine Learning Prediction of Ankle Reinjury in Individuals with Chronic Ankle Instability: A 2-Year Prospective Cohort Study with Fairness Audit.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) face a 2-year reinjury rate approaching 50%, but individualized prediction models that quantify which baseline impairments predict subsequent reinjury within an established CAI cohort remain scarce, and existing prediction models for ankle injury have not assessed sex-related fairness. The aim was to develop and internally validate sex-equitable machine learning (ML) models predicting 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, identify the most influential baseline prognostic markers, and audit sex-stratified model performance.
METHODS: One hundred physically active individuals (50 male, 50 female) with CAI (mean age 21.8 ± 2.3 years) were recruited from a university population between February 2017 and February 2018 and prospectively followed for 2 years; 96 (49 male, 47 female) with at least one follow-up response were retained for analysis (41 reinjury events, 43% reinjury rate). Fourteen baseline predictors spanning demographic, anthropometric, injury-history, patient-reported, biomechanical, postural-control, and functional-performance domains were collected. Six algorithms were trained with nested cross-validation: an unpenalized logistic regression baseline and five ML algorithms (Elastic Net, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Predictive contribution of each feature was quantified using Shapley additive explanations and partial-dependence plots. A pre-specified fairness audit compared single global and sex-specific Youden thresholds derived out-of-fold using the equalized-odds gap and disproportionate-impact ratio.
RESULTS: All algorithms achieved area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.70; Elastic Net was selected as the primary model (AUC = 0.807, 95% CI 0.714-0.893; calibration slope = 1.015). Sex, arch height index, previous sprains, dorsiflexion range of motion, and Biodex Overall Stability Index consistently emerged as the most influential prognostic markers. Within-sex discrimination was comparable between males and females, but a single global threshold produced an equalized-odds gap of 0.384 that was reduced by 57% (to 0.164) through sex-specific thresholding without retraining the model.
CONCLUSIONS: ML models with a fairness-audited threshold strategy predicted 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, reducing the equalized-odds gap by 57%, though the disproportionate-impact ratio (0.683) remained below the 0.80 benchmark. External validation is required before clinical deployment.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.
