title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Safety of Tendon-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cell Therapy in Equine Tendon and Ligament Injuries.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Equine tendinopathies and desmopathies are common musculoskeletal disorders characterized by a limited regenerative capacity and a high risk of recurrence. Tendon-derived mesenchymal stem cells (TDSCs) represent a promising regenerative therapy due to their immunomodulatory and pro-regenerative properties.
OBJECTIVES: This preliminary prospective clinical study aimed to evaluate the safety and potential efficacy of allogeneic post-mortem TDSCs, for the treatment of superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT) and suspensory ligament (SL) injuries in horses.
METHODS: Nine horses were monitored longitudinally for up to 18 months following intralesional TDSC injection. Clinical outcome was assessed using subjective lameness evaluation, objective locomotion analysis with inertial sensors and standardized ultrasonographic examinations.
RESULTS: The treatment was well tolerated, with no major adverse effects, supporting the low immunogenicity of allogeneic TDSCs. Overall clinical improvement was observed during the follow-up period and was consistent with improved locomotor symmetry measured objectively. Ultrasonographic findings suggested favorable tissue remodeling, including a reduction in hypoechoic lesions and progressive reorganization of the fibrillar architecture. However, treatment responses were heterogeneous, with SDFT lesions showing earlier clinical and ultrasonographic improvement than SL lesions. Nevertheless, this trend was not reflected in long-term outcomes, as only two horses, both presenting SL lesions, returned to their previous level of competition without reported recurrence.
CONCLUSION: Allogeneic TDSCs appear to be a safe and promising therapeutic approach for equine tendon and ligament injuries. Nevertheless, their ability to reduce long-term recurrence remains uncertain and should be investigated in larger controlled clinical trials.

title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture.
DESIGN: Systematic review.
DATA SOURCES: Web of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Human genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: 19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: COL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.

title: Cooling and exercise performance in adult men at ≥30°C: a task-stratified systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
abstract: This review evaluated cooling effects on self-paced, time-to-exhaustion and intermittent/repeated-sprint performance in adult men exercising in controlled environments at ≥30°C. Six bibliographic sources were searched from inception to 22 September 2026. Within-participant cooling-control comparisons were analysed separately by task using paired Hedges' g and correlated three-level random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood and t-based inference. Population, cooling timing and relative humidity were exploratory moderators. Sensitivity analyses varied the assumed correlations and omitted one sampling cluster at a time. Fifty-one reports contributed 80 effects from 50 sampling clusters and 480 participants after accounting for documented overlap. Cooling was associated with better self-paced performance (g = 0.24, 95% CI 0.11-0.36; I2 = 8.5%), longer time to exhaustion (g = 0.57, 95% CI 0.28-0.85; I2 = 72.9%) and better intermittent/repeated-sprint performance (g = 0.20, 95% CI 0.06-0.35; I2 ≈ 0%). No between-subgroup difference was detected in the analysed subsets (all nominal p ≥ 0.071). Model-based confidence intervals remained above zero in the specified correlation and leave-one-cluster-out analyses. Cooling was associated with small average benefits for self-paced and intermittent/repeated-sprint performance and a longer time to exhaustion. Heterogeneity and sparse subgroups limit comparisons of protocols and participant groups. These task-specific estimates do not rank cooling methods or guarantee individual benefit. title: Minimally Invasive Zadek Osteotomy vs Open Achilles Debridement for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy in Athletes: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common cause of posterior heel pain in athletic populations and may require surgical intervention following failed conservative management. Minimally invasive Zadek osteotomy (MIS Zadek) has emerged as an alternative to traditional open Achilles tendon debridement with Haglund resection, with potential advantages in recovery and complication profile.
METHODS: A retrospective comparative cohort study was performed including 50 athletic patients with IAT (25 MIS Zadek, 25 open surgery) treated between 2022 and 2024 at a single high-volume centre. All patients participated in regular sports activity and failed at least 6 months of nonoperative treatment. The primary outcome was time to return to sport. Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport rate, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) physical function (PF), PROMIS pain interference (PI), and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders.
RESULTS: Return to sport was achieved in 100% of MIS patients (25/25) and 92% of open patients (23/25; P = .49). Time to return to sport was shorter following MIS Zadek (4.3 ± 1.2 vs 6.1 ± 1.5 months; mean difference -1.8 months, 95% CI -2.6 to -1.0; P < .001). MIS remained independently associated with faster return to sport (adjusted β = -1.6 months, 95% CI -2.4 to -0.8; P < .001). Both groups showed substantial and clinically meaningful improvements in PROMIS outcomes. At 6 months, PROMIS PF was higher in the MIS group (56.5 ± 5.8 vs 52.3 ± 6.4; mean difference +4.2, 95% CI 0.6-7.8; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.69), with a similar pattern for PROMIS PI (47.2 ± 5.5 vs 51.1 ± 6.0; mean difference -3.9, 95% CI -7.1 to -0.7; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.67). By 18 months, PROMIS PF improved further in both groups with comparable outcomes (59.4 ± 4.9 vs 57.8 ± 5.2; mean difference +1.6, 95% CI -1.4 to 4.6; P = .29), and PROMIS PI similarly converged (44.8 ± 4.9 vs 46.3 ± 5.1; mean difference -1.5, 95% CI -4.4 to 1.4; P = .30). Complication rates were lower in the MIS group (2/25, 8%) compared with the open group (6/25, 24%; P = .25), although this difference did not reach statistical significance.
CONCLUSION: MIS Zadek osteotomy was associated with faster return to sport and improved early recovery compared with open surgery; with the numbers available, no significant difference in long-term functional outcomes could be detected. Complications were numerically less frequent following MIS Zadek osteotomy, although this difference did not reach statistical significanceLevel of Evidence:Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years.
OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation.
RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate.
CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement in American football athletes: examining factors associated with outcomes at a mean follow-up time of 6.3 years.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAIS) is a common cause of hip pain and performance limitation in athletes. Hip arthroscopy is the gold standard of treatment in professional American football athletes, with numerous studies demonstrating favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport (RTS) rates. However, limited outcomes data exists in collegiate athletes and fewer still in high school athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term patient-reported outcomes (PROs), RTS rates, and predictors of outcomes following hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS in high school and collegiate football athletes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed which included high-school and collegiate football athletes who underwent hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS. Outcomes were assessed using the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), International Hip Outcome Tool-12 (IHOT-12), and Hip Outcomes Score-Sport Specific Subscale (HOS-Sport). Data regarding return to preinjury sport were also collected. Pre-operative radiographic data, including alpha angle, lateral center edge angle, and Tönnis grade, were collected.
RESULTS: This cohort had a mean post-operative follow up of 6.3 years, with mean PRO scores of 82.2 on the mHHS, 84.6 on the iHOT-12, and 88.3 on the HOS-Sport. PASS thresholds were achieved by 69%, 77% and 80% of athletes for the same outcomes, respectively. 60% of the cohort attempted to return to sport, and 91% of the athletes who attempted to return to preinjury level of sport were successful. Increased age at time of surgery and larger pre-operative alpha angles were associated with worse PRO scores at follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Hip arthroscopy for FAIS in high school and collegiate football players yielded favorable long-term outcomes and RTS rates. This is similar to current outcomes data in professional athletes. Increased alpha angle and age at surgery were associated with worse outcomes, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and appropriate surgical treatment. Comparisons of outcomes between blocking and nonblocking positions may warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

title: Optimizing Post-operative Analgesia for Early Rehabilitation after Orthopedic Knee Surgery: A Randomized Comparison of Adductor Canal, Infiltration between the Popliteal Artery and Capsule of the Posterior Knee and Genicular Nerve Blocks.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Orthopedic knee surgery, including anterior cruciate ligament tear repair, patellar fracture fixation, and surgery for knee osteoarthritis, is often followed by moderate to severe pain that delays early mobilization, quadriceps activation, and physiotherapy. Motor-sparing, opioid-sparing analgesia is therefore preferred. Ultrasound-guided adductor canal block (ACB), infiltration between the popliteal artery and capsule of the posterior knee (IPACK) block, and genicular nerve block (GNB) are three such options, but direct comparisons in orthopedic knee surgery are limited.
AIMS: To compare the post-operative analgesic efficacy of ultrasound-guided ACB, IPACK block, and GNB in patients undergoing knee surgeries under subarachnoid block.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective, randomized, single-blind comparative study was conducted in the Department of Anaesthesiology, N.S.C.B. Medical College and Hospital, Jabalpur, over 18 months after institutional ethics committee approval (IEC/2023/7335-1). Ninety-nine ASA physical status I-II patients aged 18-60 years scheduled for elective knee surgery were randomized equally into three groups (n = 33 each). Group A received ultrasound-guided ACB, Group I received ultrasound-guided IPACK block, and Group G received ultrasound-guided GNB. Each block was performed with 20 mL of 0.375% ropivacaine, followed by standardized spinal anesthesia. Post-operative pain was assessed using a Visual Analog Scale (VAS) over 24 h. Time to rescue intravenous paracetamol, tramadol requirement, and block-related complications were recorded.
RESULTS: Baseline demographic characteristics were comparable among groups. Group G had lower mean VAS scores at most post-operative time points, including 16, 20 and 24 h. The time to first rescue paracetamol was longest in Group G (5.87 ± 0.43 h), followed by Group A (5.62 ± 0.48 h) and Group I (5.42 ± 0.49 h). The second paracetamol dose was also delayed the longest in Group G (11.79 ± 0.83 h). Tramadol was required in 6.06% of patients in Group G, compared with 21.21% in Group A and 30.30% in Group I.
CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing orthopedic knee surgery, all three ultrasound-guided motor-sparing blocks provided clinically useful post-operative analgesia. GNB was associated with lower pain scores at most intervals, delayed rescue analgesic requirement, and reduced tramadol use compared with ACB and IPACK block, making it a promising option to support early rehabilitation. Larger adequately powered trials with procedure-specific subgroup analysis and functional outcomes, such as quadriceps strength and range of motion, are warranted.

title: Musculoskeletal Health in Elite Athletes With Bilateral Lower Limb Loss: The ADVANCE Cohort Study.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Lower limb (LL) loss can be detrimental to bone and joint health. Exercise improves musculoskeletal outcomes in individuals without LL loss, but with limited investigation after LL loss. The aim is to assess differences in bone and joint health between elite athletes and nonathletes with bilateral LL loss to assess associations between exercise and musculoskeletal health in this population.
DESIGN: ADVANCE (Armed Services Trauma Rehabilitation Outcome) is a longitudinal cohort study involving UK military personnel and veterans who served in Afghanistan.
METHODS: Sixty-four ambulatory participants with bilateral LL loss were included. Seven participants were elite athletes (athlete group; n = 7) and were compared with the remaining participants (nonathlete group, n = 57). The Kellgren-Lawrence score for knee and hip osteoarthritis (OA), femoral neck and lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, International Physical Activity Questionnaire, and 6-minute walk test distance were compared. Outcomes were also compared between the Athlete group and Nonathlete group split by activity level.
RESULTS: Participants were 33.1 ± 4.7 years old and 6.9 ± 1.5 years postinjury. No Athlete group participants had knee OA compared with 51.8% of Nonathlete participants. There was a weak trend for more prevalent hip OA in the Nonathlete group (P = .074); 7.1% Athlete group participants and 30.7% Nonathlete group participants had Kellgren-Lawrence score ≥ 1. Femoral neck BMD was not different between groups, but there was a trend for lower lumbar spine BMD in the Nonathlete group compared with the Athlete group (-0.41 vs 0.57; P = .06). More active nonathletes had better femoral neck t scores than less active nonathletes, P = .03. Neither Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Pain, Symptoms, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, nor 6-minute walk test distance were different between groups.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and active nonathletes with LL loss may have favorable BMD profiles. Athletes with LL loss have lower prevalence of radiographic hip and knee OA. Although not conclusive due to our study design, this suggests that exercise may be associated with beneficial musculoskeletal health outcomes in this population.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Associations between demographic characteristics and Big Five personality traits after anterior cruciate ligament injury: A registry-based cross-sectional study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to investigate associations between demographic characteristics and personality traits, measured with the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2), in patients after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. A secondary exploratory purpose was to compare demographic characteristics across groups defined by predominant personality trait.
METHODS: Data for this cross-sectional study were obtained from a Swedish rehabilitation-specific registry. Patients aged 15-65 years who completed the Swedish version of the BFI-2 were included. The five BFI-2 domains (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, open-mindedness and negative emotionality) were analysed as continuous outcomes using multivariable linear regression with sex, age at injury or ACL reconstruction, body mass index (BMI), number of ACL injuries and preinjury Tegner activity level as predictors. Predominant personality trait groups were compared in a secondary exploratory analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 782 patients were included, of whom 692 had complete data for the regression analyses. Female sex was associated with higher scores in all five BFI-2 domains (all p ≤ 0.045). Older age was associated with higher extraversion, conscientiousness and open-mindedness and lower negative emotionality (all p ≤ 0.006). Higher BMI was associated with lower conscientiousness (p = 0.004) and higher open-mindedness (p = 0.049). The models explained 2.7%-13.0% of the variance in personality scores. In the secondary analysis, Agreeableness was the most common predominant trait, and patients classified as predominantly open-minded were older than patients in the other groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Sex and age were associated with several BFI-2 personality traits after ACL injury, whereas BMI showed only small associations. However, demographic characteristics explained little of the variance in personality scores, indicating that personality cannot be reliably inferred from demographic characteristics alone.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Pain Management in Elective Orthopaedic Surgery: A Delphi Consensus of the Academic Orthopaedic Consortium.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pain management is a critical component of orthopaedic care, aimed at minimizing discomfort, facilitating recovery, and enhancing functional outcomes. The purpose of this study was to establish consensus statements through the Delphi process on pain management from preoperatively to postoperatively at the time of elective orthopaedic sports medicine and arthroplasty surgery.
METHODS: A consensus process using the Delphi technique was conducted. Thirty-seven orthopaedic surgeons, anaesthesiologist pain management physicians, and musculoskeletal researchers participated in these consensus statements. Consensus was defined as achieving 80 to 89% agreement, strong consensus was defined as 90 to 99% agreement, and unanimous consensus was indicated by 100% agreement with a proposed statement.
RESULTS: Of the 40 total questions and consensus statements in this group, four achieved unanimous consensus, 21 achieved strong consensus, 14 achieved consensus, and one did not reach any consensus.
CONCLUSION: The majority of statements reached some degree of consensus, with most achieving at least strong consensus. The statements that achieved unanimous consensus were on preoperative patient counselling for those with opioid addiction risk factors, including preoperative plans, preoperative education, frank discussions on expectations of pain after surgery, and pain management contracts. In addition, unanimous consensus was achieved that practices should have a standard opioid prescribing protocol to minimize prescribing, based on the procedure performed and with a maximum prescribing amount, and regarding the advantages of e-prescribing for opioids. Finally, unanimous consensus was determined that acetaminophen is always indicated, except when there is a medical contraindication such as liver impairment.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Orthopedic Surgeon and Primary Care Orthopedic Physician Preferences for Sports Participation for Cast-Immobilized Healing Fractures: A Survey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: No published clinical practice guidelines outlining recommended activity restrictions were found for patients with cast-immobilized healing fractures; wide variations in practice exist. This survey aimed to elucidate physician/surgeon preferences for sports participation for patients with short arm cast-immobilized distal radial metaphyseal fractures.
METHODS: Attending orthopedic surgeons, physiatrists, and primary care sports medicine physicians at a single urban tertiary-care orthopedic hospital were invited to complete an anonymous survey with up to 26 questions from 5/2023-7/2023. Descriptive statistics were done. Pearson Chi-Square tests compared pediatric surgeons to all other providers.
RESULTS: One hundred twenty physicians and surgeons were invited to participate. Response rate was 43% (51/120); 59% (30/51) reported treating distal radial fractures with casting and were invited to complete the remaining survey; 70% (21/30) allow return to sports while casted. For respondents permitting sports/activity participation, factors impacting this decision included longer healing time from injury, minimal displacement, greater radiographic healing, and older age at the time of injury. Type of activity, effect on quality of life, level of competition, effect on college/team recruitment, and patient and parental pressure were noted factors impacting activity recommendations. Comparing pediatric orthopedic surgeons with all other providers, there was no notable difference in proportion permitting return to sport/activity in cast (63% vs. 73%, P = 0.67).
CONCLUSION: For cast-immobilized healing fractures of the distal radius, many physicians/surgeons permit sport/activity participation in some capacity, with multiple variables impacting providers preference for activity restrictions. Clinical practice guidelines delineating activity restrictions for cast-immobilized fractures should be developed.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Greater eccentric hamstrings to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with reduced odds of revision within 2 years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between eccentric hamstrings-to-concentric quadriceps strength ratio (mixed hamstrings to quadriceps [HQ]-strength ratio) at 6 months postoperatively and revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACL-R) within 2 years of primary surgery. The secondary purpose was to investigate the association between the mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance limb symmetry index (LSI).
METHODS: Data were collected from a local registry at Capio Artro Clinic, Stockholm, Sweden. Patients aged ≥15 years, without concomitant ligament injuries and meniscal resection or repair who underwent primary ACL-R with hamstring tendon autografts between 2005 and 2021 were included. Isokinetic eccentric hamstrings and concentric quadriceps strength were assessed using a Biodex dynamometer 6 months postoperatively. Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg and revision ACL-R were analysed using multivariable logistic regression analysis, presented with odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC). Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance LSI were analysed with linear regression.
RESULTS: Of the 3458 patients included, 49.5% were female and the mean age was 28.8 ± 10.4 years. Patients who underwent revision ACL-R within 2 years had lower mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg 6 months postoperatively. After adjustment for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level, each 10-unit increase in the mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg was associated with lower odds of revision ACL-R (OR = 0.81, 95% CI [0.71;0.93], p = 0.003). However, the discriminatory ability was poor (AUC = 0.64). A greater mixed HQ-strength ratio was associated with poorer single-leg hop for distance LSI, adjusted for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level (β = -1.30, 95% CI [-1.51;-1.09], p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The mixed HQ-strength ratio may complement the evaluation of muscle strength recovery after ACL-R. However, its poor discriminatory ability limits its use to identify patients who will undergo revision ACL-R.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee positive work (generation) and jump height.
METHODS: Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations.
RESULTS: Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006).
CONCLUSION: Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and return-to-sport research.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Comparison of immediate post-operative pain and functional outcomes of surgeon-administered adductor canal block through subvastus versus medial parapatellar approach in total knee arthroplasty: A retrospective comparative study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Post-operative pain significantly impedes early rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The adductor canal block (ACB) provides effective analgesia with minimal quadriceps impairment. This study compares immediate post-operative pain and functional outcomes of surgeon-administered ACB through subvastus (SV) versus medial parapatellar (MP) approaches.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective comparative study conducted between January 2024 and March 2025, medical records of 60 patients who underwent unilateral primary TKA were reviewed. Patients were grouped based on the surgical approach used for intraoperative surgeon-administered ACB (30 SV, 30 MP). A modified anatomical technique was used in all cases. A standardized multimodal non-opioid post-operative analgesic protocol was used in both groups. Outcomes assessed at 12 h post-operatively included Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), timed up and go (TUG) test, and range of motion (ROM). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 8.4.2.
RESULT: Both groups demonstrated significant post-operative improvement in pain and function. The SV group achieved superior pain control (post-operative VAS 3.52 ± 0.69 vs. 4.38 ± 0.82; P = 0.0001), better functional outcomes (WOMAC 60.1 vs. 72.17; P < 0.0001), and faster TUG times (P = 0.0104). ROM improvements were significant in both groups, with no statistically significant intergroup difference.
CONCLUSION: In this retrospective comparative study, the SV approach with surgeon-administered ACB was associated with better immediate post-operative analgesia and functional outcomes than the MP approach. The study cannot determine whether these differences were attributable to the surgical approach, ACB delivery, or both. Larger prospective, randomized studies with longer follow-up are warranted.

title: Study of Transdermal Buprenorphine Patch versus Oral Etoricoxib for Postoperative Pain Management after Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Randomized Comparative Open-label Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is a widely performed procedure for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, providing significant pain relief, improved joint function, and better quality of life. However, it is associated with substantial postoperative pain, which may delay mobilization, impair rehabilitation, prolong hospital stay, and increase the risk of chronic postoperative pain, thus making effective perioperative analgesia crucial for achieving optimal postoperative outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of transdermal buprenorphine patch versus oral etoricoxib for postoperative pain management in patients undergoing TKA, using Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores at rest and during movement for up to 1 week.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This randomized comparative study enrolled 88 patients of American Society of Anesthesiologists grade I/II after ethical approval. The patients were randomly allocated into two groups of 44 patients each. In Group A, patients received oral etoricoxib (90 mg), 1 h before surgery with a sip of water, and in Group B, patients received a transdermal buprenorphine patch (10 µg/h), 12 h before surgery. For statistical analysis, the Chi-square test and Student's t-test were used.
RESULTS: Statistically significant differences were observed in VAS scores (at rest and during movement), with Group B demonstrating significantly lower pain. Furthermore, rescue analgesic requirements and length of hospital stay were reduced significantly in Group B, thus indicating overall superior postoperative pain control.
CONCLUSION: Transdermal buprenorphine patch offers sustained analgesia (reduced VAS scores) with the potential for fewer systemic side effects, reduced need for additional opioid and rescue analgesic requirements, leading to shorter length of hospital stay.

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus.
abstract: The extensor digitorum longus muscle and tendons are among the longer muscle-tendon units in the lower leg and foot. This feather-like, unipennate muscle is part of the anterior ankle group, attaching proximally along the lateral side of the lateral condyle of the tibia and the upper three-quarters of the fibula's inner surface. Near the ankle, the tendon narrows as it passes beneath the extensor retinacula and divides into four smaller tendons that connect to the toes. Since it crosses the ankle joint and attaches to the second through fifth toes, it facilitates dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toe joints. An accurate diagnosis of extensor digitorum longus tendonitis or rupture is crucial for appropriate treatment planning and optimal patient outcomes. Diagnostic musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSKUS) has become a widely used imaging modality for assessing many ankle and foot pathologies. It offers a portable, real-time, and cost-effective alternative that is gaining traction in rehabilitation and sports medicine settings. MSKUS has emerged as a valuable, non-invasive imaging modality for evaluating ankle and foot injuries. This manuscript reviews the utility of MSKUS in evaluating the quality, size, sonographic techniques, and clinical implications for rehabilitation professionals who need to visualize the extensor digitorum longus. By integrating MSKUS into clinical practice, providers can improve diagnostic accuracy, increase diagnostic confidence, monitor healing progression, and guide rehabilitation strategies to optimize outcomes for patients with ankle and foot injuries.

title: Horizontal and Multidirectional Single-Leg Hop Tests Predict Isokinetic Quadriceps and Hamstring Strengths After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), isokinetic strength and single-leg hop tests (SLHT) are used to assess return to sport readiness. This study examined the relationships and predictive effects of isokinetic knee extension (Ex) and flexion (Flx) strength with 5 SLHTs at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR.
HYPOTHESIS: There would be significant correlation between knee Ex and Flx strengths on the operated side and 5 different SLHTs; SLHTs would significantly predict knee isokinetic Ex and Flx strength.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Fifty-one male participants underwent unilateral ACLR. Lysholm, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), and Tegner scales were assessed preoperatively and 6 to 8 months postoperatively. At the same follow-up, isokinetic strength at 60°/s, 180°/s, and 240°/s and 5 SLHTs were tested on both limbs. Data were analyzed with paired t tests, Pearson correlations, Fisher's exact test, and simple linear regression; limb symmetry index (LSI) cut-off was ≥85%.
RESULTS: Isokinetic strength and single-leg hop (SH), crossover hop, and medial side triple-hop (TH) distances did not differ significantly between limbs (P > 0.05), whereas TH and 90° medial rotation hop distances were significantly shorter on the operated side (P < 0.05). Participants' Lysholm and IKDC scores improved significantly at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR (P < 0.001), but Tegner activity level did not change significantly (P > 0.05). High correlation was found between Ex strength at 60°/s and SH and TH distances on the operated side, and high-moderate correlations were found at 180°/s and 240°/s. Flx strengths showed a similar but slightly lower degree of correlation. Simple linear regression models revealed that especially SH and TH distances significantly predicted both Ex and Flx strengths (adjusted R2 0.26-0.52; P < 0.001). Among the LSI values, only a significant correlation was found between 60°/s Ex and TH LSI ratio (P = 0.01).
CONCLUSION: The findings show that SH and TH tests were highly predictive of isokinetic knee strength after ACLR.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SLHTs after ACLR can be used as a practical and accessible complement to isokinetic measurements.

title: Different osteoarthritis progression rates within early-stage knee osteoarthritis: a retrospective cohort study using machine learning cluster analysis from the osteoarthritis initiative database.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disease with varying progression rates among patients within the same severity grade. This study aimed to identify clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes among knees with baseline Kellgren and Lawrence (KL) grade 2 osteoarthritis and to compare their 4-year radiographic progression patterns using baseline radiographic features, lifetime exercise patterns, and demographic characteristics.
METHODS: Data of patients with baseline KL grade 2 from the Osteoarthritis Initiative database were retrieved. Unsupervised clustering was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) for dimensionality reduction, followed by hierarchical density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (HDBSCAN) to identify distinct subgroups. The proportion of knees progressing to KL grade ≥ 3 within 4 years was compared between subgroups, followed by a survival analysis until knee replacement or progression to KL grade 4.
RESULTS: A total of 1997 knees with a mean follow-up of 103.3 months (maximum, 108 months) were included. A total of seven subgroups were identified and classified into accelerated osteoarthritis progression (AOP) group and slow osteoarthritis progression (SOP) group according to whether their 4-year KL grade progression proportions were above or below the training-set average. In a supportive long-term survival analysis, the AOP group also showed significantly earlier progression to knee replacement or KL grade 4 than the SOP group (training set, P < 0.001; test set, P = 0.049), although the absolute difference in mean survival time was modest (8.3 versus 8.5 years in the training set; 8.4 versus 8.6 years in the test set). The AOP group was characterized mainly by lateral joint space narrowing (JSN) and medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, whereas the SOP group was characterized by medial JSN without subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant patterns without JSN, or chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns; these differences were statistically significant across clusters.
CONCLUSIONS: Within baseline KL grade 2 knees, clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes, including lateral JSN, medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant changes without JSN, and chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns, were associated with different 4-year KL grade progression rates. These findings support viewing KL grade 2 knee OA as a heterogeneous radiographic stage that may be further stratified into phenotype-based subgroups with different short-term radiographic prognoses.

title: Breast Injuries in Women's Rugby Union: A Comparison of Prospective and Retrospective Surveillance.
abstract: Retrospective research has reported a high prevalence of breast injuries in women's rugby union (RU); however, most injuries are not reported to medical staff. This study compared the incidence and severity of breast injuries collected both prospectively and retrospectively over a comparable match exposure period. Prospective surveillance was conducted by clinicians (n = 14) using an online injury surveillance system across 140 RU players. Retrospective surveillance was conducted using an anonymous online survey completed by 370 RU players. Injury incidence was calculated per 1000 hours of match exposure. Severity was assessed using breast pain, bruising and swelling, ability to continue play, perceived effect on performance, and long-term breast changes. Three breast injuries were prospectively recorded over 1204 hours of competition (2.5 injuries/1000 hours). In contrast, 144 breast injuries were reported retrospectively over 5055 hours of competition (28.5 injuries/1000 hours). The retrospective injury rate was significantly higher than the prospective rate (IRR = 11.4, 95% CI: 3.15-41.73; p < 0.002). Ninety-six percent (n = 139) of retrospectively reported injuries had not been disclosed to medical staff. Injury severity was similar between surveillance methods, with bruising commonly reported, all players continuing to participate despite injury, and over half perceiving a negative effect on performance. Long-term breast changes were reported by 6% (n = 8) of players. The substantially lower incidence recorded prospectively suggests that breast injuries are underreported in women's RU. Improved reporting and surveillance strategies are required to better capture breast injuries and support female athlete health and performance.

title: Infrared thermography reveals differences in thigh skin-temperature trajectories during early recovery after four cycling protocols.
abstract: Exercise intensity or mode alters metabolic heat production, blood-flow distribution, and heat dissipation, but the evolution of these thermal responses during early recovery remains unclear. In this randomized crossover study, 19 adults (10 men, 9 women) completed low-intensity continuous cycling (E1), moderate-intensity continuous cycling (E2), high-intensity intervals (E3), and all-out sprint intervals (E4). Infrared thermography measured average skin temperature (aTsk) in a standardized thigh region through 15 min of recovery. At 15 min, changes from each session's baseline were -0.12, +0.13, -1.19, and -1.86 °C after E1-E4, respectively. The condition-by-stage interaction was significant (F(5.45, 92.68) = 17.38, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.506). Absolute aTsk was lower after E3 and E4 than after E1 by 1.04 °C (95% confidence interval 0.68-1.39) and 1.36 °C (0.98-1.74), respectively (both Bonferroni-adjusted P < 0.001). None of the condition-adjusted Pearson correlations passed FDR correction, consistent with substantial between-condition contributions. Thermograms from one participant also illustrated local surface thermal contrast. Early-recovery thermography is a candidate measure of responses to these complete cycling protocols, pending prospective within-person validation. title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Beyond Reconstruction: Return to Olympic Medal Performance Following Morphology-Informed and Criterion-Based Nonoperative Management of a Femoral-Sided Sherman Type II ACL Injury - A Case Report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: ACL reconstruction and repair remains the predominant treatment pathway for elite athletes participating in pivoting sports. However, emerging evidence suggests that selected ACL injury phenotypes may possess healing potential, while objective criteria for identifying athletes who may successfully pursue nonoperative management remain poorly defined. Data describing elite athletes returning to the highest level of competition following nonoperative treatment are particularly scarce. The purpose of this case report is to describe the morphology-informed nonoperative management, criterion-based rehabilitation, and return to Olympic-level competition of an elite field hockey player following a fermoral-sided Sherman type II ACL injury.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 30-year-old male international elite field hockey player sustained a femoral-sided Sherman II ACL injury with preserved fiber continuity and synovial sheath during an Olympic qualification tournament. MRI demonstrated a meniscal ramp lesion and bone bruise. In the absence of subjective instability, a morphology-informed nonoperative treatment strategy was selected. Rehabilitation followed a criterion-based framework guided by objective assessments of strength, neuromuscular control, movement quality, and sport-specific function rather than time-based milestones.
OUTCOMES: Comprehensive return-to-sport testing performed 86 days post injury demonstrated quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry indices of 99% and 98%, hop-test symmetry exceeding 90% and symmetrical gait mechanics. Running resumed at 73 days, unrestricted team training at 124 days, and international competition at 140 days post injury. The athlete subsequently competed in the Olympic Games final and achieved Olympic silver-medal performance 200 days after injury. Patient-reported outcomes returned to preinjury levels within 12 months. Follow-up MRI demonstrated preserved ACL continuity, ligament remodelling, and no evidence of rupture.
DISCUSSION: This case challenges the prevailing assumption that ACL reconstruction and repair are invariably required for elite pivoting-sport athletes to regain international and Olympic-level performance. It highlights the potential importance of injury morphology, shared decision-making, and objective functional assessment when selecting treatment pathways after ACL injury.
CONCLUSION: For carefully selected athletes with favorable ACL morphology, criterion-based rehabilitation combined with objective return-to-sport-assessment may represent a viable alternative pathway to reconstruction and repair. This case supports further investigation of morphology-informed and performance-oriented management strategies for ACL injuries in elite sport.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Understanding Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) is a clinical condition resulting from low energy availability that affects physiological function and performance in athletes of all genders and ages. REDs is increasingly recognized in pediatric populations, particularly in endurance, aesthetic, and weight-class sports, such as long-distance running, gymnastics, and wrestling, respectively. REDs is a multisystem condition characterized by hormonal dysfunction, low bone density, or psychological disturbances, and is associated with increased injury risk and impaired performance. Management centers on restoring energy balance through nutritional and behavioral interventions, and prevention strategies emphasize education and early recognition. This review synthesizes current evidence on REDs in adolescent athletes, emphasizing current understanding of risk factors, clinical presentation, practical approaches to evaluation and management, and prevention strategies to support pediatricians in the management of REDs in the primary care setting.

title: Fresh Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation as a Salvage Procedure Following Failed Fixation of Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Lateral Femoral Condyle: A Case Report.
abstract: BACKGROUND Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the knee can progress to large osteochondral defects when fragment fixation fails, representing a reconstructive challenge in young active patients. Fresh osteochondral allograft transplantation (OCA) restores both the viable hyaline cartilage and subchondral bone and has emerged as a joint-preserving treatment for these lesions. However, reports describing OCA as a salvage procedure after failed OCD fixation remain limited. CASE REPORT A 19-year-old female patient who participated in competitive sports presented with recurrent pain and mechanical locking of the left knee after previous fixation of an OCD lesion of the lateral femoral condyle. Imaging demonstrated fixation failure, retained hardware, loose bodies, and an osteochondral defect measuring 25×12 mm. Open removal of the failed fixation and loose bodies was followed by fresh size-matched OCA using a press-fit technique. At the 24-month follow-up, the patient had returned to high-level athletic activity without mechanical symptoms. Clinical examination demonstrated functional range of motion and adequate quadriceps strength. The International Knee Documentation Committee subjective score was 93/100, and the Tegner Activity Scale score was 7, compared with a preinjury score of 8. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed satisfactory graft incorporation without graft-related complications. CONCLUSIONS Fresh OCA may be considered as a joint-preserving salvage option after failed OCD fixation in carefully selected young patients. In this case, satisfactory graft incorporation, functional recovery, and return to preinjury recreational sports activities were observed at 24-month follow-up.

title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury induces neuroplastic changes within the central nervous system (CNS) that may persist beyond reconstruction and rehabilitation.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose was to compare neurocognitive performance and cortical oscillatory activity between open-skill athletes (eg, soccer, basketball, or handball players) without ACL injury history and athletes with ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during a probabilistic go/no-go task. It was hypothesized that athletes with ACLR would exhibit poorer behavioral performance and less efficient oscillatory dynamics, particularly higher theta and lower suppression of beta and alpha power oscillations after goal stimulus onset.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR) performed a probabilistic go/no-go task while electroencephalographic recording was performed. Time-frequency analysis targeted midfrontal theta (4-7 Hz), left-lateralized central beta (15-25 Hz), and posterior alpha (8-12 Hz) oscillations during prestimulus and target stimulus windows. Linear mixed-effects models examined group differences in cognitive performance and oscillatory power.
RESULTS: Athletes with ACLR showed slower response times and lower accuracy (d = 0.75-1.09). Midfrontal theta power was attenuated for the ACLR group during the prestimulus phase (d = 0.60) yet elevated during target phase trials (d = 0.48), indicating a shift from proactive to reactive cognitive control in athletes with ACLR. Left-lateralized central beta (d = 0.61) and posterior alpha suppression (d = 0.55) were reduced, reflecting impaired motor cortical disinhibition and less efficient visual-attentional resource deployment, especially under high uncertainty conditions.
CONCLUSION: Athletes with ACLR showed persistent alterations in the cortical oscillatory mechanisms associated with conflict monitoring, motor preparation, and attentional allocation under uncertainty. These neurocognitive alterations may compromise adaptive motor responses in sport contexts characterized by high uncertainty and cognitive mental demand, potentially increasing reinjury risk. These findings support the integration of neurocognitive assessment into return-to-sport protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Alterations in cortical oscillatory dynamics during decision-making under uncertainty may reflect reduced efficiency in cognitive control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation, which are not detected by standard assessments. Exercise professionals should consider integrating these assessments into return-to-sport protocols to address the persistent CNS alterations that may underlie reinjury risk in athletes with ACLR.
