title: Repeated sprint training in hypoxia as a post-surgical rehabilitation strategy: A case study in an elite badminton player.
abstract: Badminton is a racquet sport that imposes high demands on both aerobic and anaerobic capacity and involves repetitive, high-intensity movements, increasing the risk of non-contact injuries to joints and muscle-tendon units. Returning to sport-specific conditioning after injury, particularly post-surgery, presents challenges for deconditioned athletes seeking to restore aerobic capacity while minimising mechanical stress imposed on the injured parts. This case study evaluated the feasibility of integrating short-term repeated sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) as a supplementary modality within a late-stage post-lower back surgery rehabilitation program to support aerobic reconditioning before return to sport-specific conditioning. An elite men's singles badminton athlete completed 4-week RSH (FiO2 ~ 16.5%), alongside his regular rehabilitation schedule. The intervention consisted of 20 × 4-s all-out cycling sprints interspersed with 30-56-s recovery, performed once weekly. Post-intervention lactate profiling suggested a rightward shift in the blood lactate curve, with estimated increases of 33% and 10% in power output at the aerobic and anaerobic thresholds, respectively, indicative of aerobic reconditioning. However, the present findings should be interpreted cautiously due to observed stage-to-stage blood lactate variability, single-case design, and concurrent rehabilitation. Overall, the present study supports the feasibility of incorporating hypoxic RSH in late-stage rehabilitation to facilitate return to sport-specific conditioning.

title: Severe injuries in competitive cycling during an olympic cycle: injury patterns, time loss, and return-to-performance outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cycling is an established Olympic sport associated with a distinct injury profile that has not yet been comprehensively investigated. This study aimed to retrospectively assess and analyze severe cycling-related injuries resulting in ≥ 3 weeks of time loss over a complete Olympic cycle.
METHODS: A total of 192 cyclists were included, based on a retrospective online questionnaire assessing injury location, type, context, time loss, and return-to-sport outcomes. Comparisons by sex, discipline, and competitive level were performed at the athlete level using exact tests with 95% confidence intervals and were considered exploratory.
RESULTS: Seventy-two of 192 athletes sustained at least one severe injury over the five-year period, corresponding to a proportion of 37.5% (95% CI 31.0-44.5). A total of 237 injuries were recorded, with the upper extremity (33.8%) and lower extremity (27.8%) being the most frequently affected regions. The most common diagnoses were hand fractures (n = 14), clavicle fractures (n = 13), and non-specific knee injuries (n = 9). Hand fractures (33.3%; p = 0.002) and shoulder dislocations (20.0%; p = 0.002) were most frequent among BMX athletes, while hand fractures also occurred more frequently in competitive athletes than in recreational athletes (13.5% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.001). Clavicle fractures occurred predominantly during competition and non-specific knee injuries during training. Mean time loss ranged from 6.5 weeks for hand fractures to 13.3 weeks for shoulder dislocations. Full return to pre-injury performance ranged from 85.7% after hand fractures to 28.6% after acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations.
CONCLUSION: Injury patterns differed by discipline and setting, suggesting that prevention strategies should address both. The low rate of full return to performance after AC joint separations despite moderate time loss underlines the importance of distinguishing return to sport from return to performance in rehabilitation.

title: Case Study Insights Into Female World-Class and Elite Athletes' Training and Physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article offers a structured overview of published case studies involving elite and world-class female Olympic athletes, highlighting the unique insights these studies provide into training characteristics, physiology, performance, and female-specific factors.
METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for peer-reviewed case studies involving tiers 4 to 5 female Olympic athletes reporting individual-level data on training, physiological, and/or performance characteristics.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight studies describing 54 elite and world-class female athletes from 18 countries and 19 Olympic sports met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were published after 2017 (68%), originated from Europe (58%), and involved endurance sports (81%). Fifteen studies examined long-term athlete development, with observation periods ranging from 4 to 26 years. Fourteen studies reported annual training and physiological characteristics across 10 sports including training volume, intensity distribution, periodization, and physiological profiling. Four studies examined altitude training, 8 addressed competition demands, tapering, and precompetition strategies, and 8 focused on female-specific physiology, health, and performance, including energy availability, menstrual function, hormonal cycle monitoring and pregnancy, and postpartum return to sport.
CONCLUSION: Case studies provide unique athlete-centered insights into the complex interactions between training, physiology, health, and performance in elite female athletes. Collectively, they demonstrate that pathways to world-class performance are highly individualized, while generating hypotheses that complement group-based research. Future case studies should prioritize underrepresented sports, geographical regions, and female-specific topics to expand the diversity of performance environments and athlete populations represented in the literature.

title: Autologous Osteochondral Transplantation Remains a Reliable Option for Talar Osteochondral Lesions, With Low Knee Donor-Site Morbidity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral transplantation (AOT) is a surgical option for talar osteochondral lesions (OCL), with favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport rates; however, knee donor-site morbidity remains a concern.
PURPOSE: To evaluate clinical and functional outcomes, complications, return to work and sport, and satisfaction after AOT for talar OCL.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective case series.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients ≥18 years with talar OCL treated with AOT (2011-2022; minimum 2-year follow-up); patients with prior knee pain or surgery, infection, advanced osteoarthritis, or rheumatologic disease were excluded. Outcomes included the AOFAS hindfoot, Lysholm, and Tegner scores, ankle and knee visual analog scale (VAS) pain, satisfaction, return to work and sport, and complications.
RESULTS: Thirty-seven patients (78% male; median age, 36 years; median follow-up, 24 months) were included. Median lesion size was 150 mm², all medial; 14 (38%) had concomitant procedures. The AOFAS score improved from 54.5 to 95.8 (mean difference, 41.3; 95% CI, 38.4-44.3) and ankle VAS from 7.0 to 1.6 (-5.4; 95% CI, -5.9 to -4.9) (both p < 0.001). Postoperative Lysholm score was 98.8 ± 4.0 and knee VAS 1.2 ± 0.8 (no preoperative knee scores). Return to work took 2.3 ± 1.2 months; all 32 athletes resumed sport at 6.5 ± 2.1 months, 20 (63%) in their pre-injury sport. Tegner scores were unchanged (5.4 vs 5.5; p = 0.624). One knee hemarthrosis and one repeat ankle arthroscopy occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: AOT for talar OCL yielded favorable short-term outcomes, high return-to-work and return-to-sport rates, and low reported knee donor-site morbidity; baseline knee scores were unavailable.
LEVEL OF CLINICAL EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Using double-bundle Achilles tendon-bone allograft for reconstruction of compound loss of lateral malleolus and lateral ankle ligaments: A rare case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Composite defects of the lateral ankle, involving bone loss, ligament disruption, and soft tissue compromise, cause profound mechanical instability and are difficult to reconstruct with techniques that address bone or ligaments alone.
PATIENT CONCERNS: We report a 26-year-old woman who presented with progressive right ankle pain, recurrent giving-way, and peroneal tendon subluxation 7 years after a high-energy crush injury that required flap coverage.
DIAGNOSES: Lateral malleolar loss with a distal fibular bony defect measuring approximately 5 × 3 × 2 cm and chronic varus instability; complete anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) rupture; and peroneal tendon dislocation were confirmed by stress radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging.
INTERVENTIONS: Single-stage reconstruction with a cryopreserved Achilles tendon-bone allograft. The calcaneal bone block was contoured and fixed to the fibular stump with a 4.5-mm cannulated screw to reconstitute the lateral malleolus. The tendon was split into 2 bundles (7 mm × 30 mm for the ATFL and 7 mm × 40 mm for the CFL) for anatomic ATFL and CFL reconstruction and secured with interference screws at the talar and calcaneal footprints. The peroneal tendons were reduced after bony restoration. Postoperative rehabilitation used an Aircast® brace with non-weight-bearing ambulation for the first 3 weeks, partial weight-bearing from week 3, full weight-bearing by week 6, and brace discontinuation at week 12.
OUTCOMES: At the final follow-up of 16 months, the patient ambulated pain-free with a stable ankle. Radiographs demonstrated successful incorporation of the bone allograft, and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed intact ATFL/CFL grafts with maintained peroneal tendon reduction. Functional scores were Karlsson-Peterson 87 and American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society ankle-hindfoot 90.
LESSONS: A double-bundle Achilles tendon-bone allograft enables simultaneous reconstruction of lateral malleolar bone and lateral ligaments, avoiding donor-site morbidity and achieving durable stability in complex, previously reconstructed ankles. This approach should be considered when both osseous and ligamentous deficits coexist.

title: Maximum-Effort Jumping Exposes the Achilles Tendon to High Strain and Indicates Potential Overload in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract: Plyometric exercise is a fundamental component of many sport disciplines and may overload the Achilles tendon (AT) by subjecting it to high strain magnitudes. AT strain profiles were investigated during countermovement, drop, hurdle, and horizontal single-leg jumps - common plyometric exercises - in order to assess exercise-induced AT loading. This was done by measuring AT elongation during the jumps using reflective markers on the skin to reconstruct the AT path, while the myotendinous junction of the gastrocnemius medialis was recorded using ultrasound in 18 adolescent athletes. Electromyographic (EMG) activity of the tibialis anterior, soleus, gastrocnemius medialis and lateralis muscles, kinematics, and ground reaction forces were also measured. Although the maximum resultant ankle joint moment differed significantly between the investigated jumps, maximum AT strain and EMG activity of the triceps surae muscles were invariant between jump types. On average, the maximum AT strains ranged from 9.0% to 10.7%, and the EMG activity ranged from 0.96 to 1.43 times the maximum EMG activity achieved during a maximum voluntary fixed-end plantar flexion contraction, across the jumps. The consistently high AT strain magnitudes across the investigated jumps highlight the substantial mechanical demand placed on the AT during maximum-effort jumping tasks, which exceed the reported effective strain range for tendon adaptation. The frequent application of plyometric exercises involving such high-magnitude strains in training practice may contribute to AT overload in adolescent athletes.

title: Editorial Commentary: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Requires the Right Patient, the Right Dose, and the Right Time.
abstract: Quadriceps weakness is a persistent challenge after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. When used as an adjunct to rehabilitation, neuromuscular electrical stimulation can aid in quadriceps strength recovery. However, optimizing the clinical application of neuromuscular electrical stimulation requires consideration of the right patient, the right dose, and the right time. Volitional activation failure can limit adequate voluntary loading of the quadriceps, particularly in the early postoperative period. Although the evidence supports early neuromuscular electrical stimulation use when activation deficits are most pronounced, treatment should be guided by resolution of underlying impairments rather than postoperative time alone.

title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects.
METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented.
RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program.
CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

title: Sports-related peripheral neuropathies in athletes: mechanisms, imaging evaluation, and sport-specific patterns.
abstract: Peripheral neuropathy in athletes is increasingly recognized as a significant source of morbidity, with injury patterns varying according to the biomechanical demands of specific sports. Although peripheral nerve disorders in athletes may result from acute trauma, they more commonly arise from chronic, repetitive mechanical stress inherent to athletic activity. Despite their frequency, they frequently remain underdiagnosed, as clinical manifestations often overlap with other musculoskeletal disorders. Mechanisms of injury include compression, traction, laceration, ischemia, and repetitive microtrauma. Distinct athletic modalities are associated with characteristic neuropathies reflecting sport-specific kinematics and loading patterns. Awareness of these biomechanical factors and recognition of typical clinical presentations are essential for accurate assessment of athletes with suspected nerve injury. Diagnostic evaluation frequently requires advanced imaging modalities, particularly magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) and high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS), which enable detailed structural assessment of peripheral nerves and detection of secondary imaging findings. Electrodiagnostic studies may provide complementary functional information in selected cases. Early and precise diagnosis is critical to guide management, facilitate safe return to sport, and prevent long-term functional deficits. While most nerve disorders respond to conservative treatment, severe, progressive, or refractory cases may warrant surgical intervention to restore function and enable return to play (RTP). This review examines mechanisms of injury, clinical evaluation, classification systems, imaging findings, and sport-specific patterns of peripheral nerve injury across diverse athletic disciplines.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Exostosis of the sustentaculum tali causing tibiotarsal joint pathology in a Standardbred racehorse trotter.
abstract: This report describes a novel case of exostosis on the medial aspect of the sustentaculum tali, (ST) associated with tibiotarsal joint (TTJ) pathology, without involvement of the tarsal sheath or lateral digital flexor tendon. A 5-year-old Standardbred gelding was presented with right TTJ effusion and exercise-induced hind-limb lameness. Diagnostic imaging identified a columnar periosteal proliferation on the medial ST, accompanied by synovial effusion and joint capsule thickening; however, the tarsal sheath and lateral digital flexor tendon remained unremarkable. Although TTJ arthroscopy confirmed synovitis, it did not allow visualization of the exostosis. The lesion was successfully excised via an ultrasound-guided extra-articular surgical approach. Postoperative management included a structured rehabilitation program, resulting in a return to full-speed training by Day 76 with no recurrence of lameness. Follow-up evaluations demonstrated improved performance and complete resolution of TTJ effusion and associated swelling. This case highlighted the importance of multimodal imaging in identifying extra-synovial lesions of the ST and supported ultrasound-guided extra-articular removal as an effective surgical option for ST exostosis. Although the underlying cause of the lesion was uncertain, subclinical trauma was considered a likely contributing factor. Key clinical message: The ST is a horizontal bony projection on the plantaromedial aspect of the calcaneus. Due to its minimal soft-tissue coverage, it is particularly vulnerable to external trauma and subsequent osseous proliferation. Exostosis of the ST may result in impingement of the plantaromedial pouch of the tarsocrural (tibiotarsal) joint, contributing to joint irritation and secondary pathology. Accurate diagnosis and effective case management rely on the combined use of radiography and ultrasonography, which together enable detailed assessment of both osseous changes and associated soft-tissue structures.

title: A mechanically active microneedle platform integrated with engineered exosomes for enhanced tendon-bone regeneration.
abstract: Functional regeneration of the tendon-bone interface remains a major challenge because early healing is constrained by an adverse inflammatory microenvironment and insufficient mechanical cues. Here, we developed a mechano-regenerative strategy that combines YAP-primed engineered exosomes with localized biomaterial-based delivery and active mechanical stimulation. Exosomes derived from a YAP agonist (PY-60) preconditioned TDSCs (P-Exo) showed enhanced uptake and promoted the osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, accompanied by activation of YAP-associated signaling and PI3K-Akt-related pathways. To improve local retention, P-Exo were incorporated into a ROS-responsive adhesive hydrogel, which accelerated fibrocartilage formation, bone ingrowth, and biomechanical restoration in a rabbit tendon-bone healing model. To address more complex repair conditions, we engineered a three-layer self-contracting microneedle platform for deep-tissue delivery of P-Exo with concurrent active mechanical stimulation. In an infected rat rotator cuff model, this system reduced bacterial burden and oxidative stress, promoted a reparative macrophage polarization and angiogenesis, and improved tendon-bone structural regeneration, biomechanical strength, and functional recovery. Together, these findings support a therapeutic framework in which engineered exosome signaling and active mechanoregulation act in concert to enhance tendon-bone repair.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Unpacking the Success: An Ecological Systems Perspective on Distance Running Performance in Ethiopia.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study employed a mixed-methods approach grounded in Ecological Systems Theory to investigate factors contributing to Ethiopia's dominance in distance running.
METHODS: Data were collected from 145 Ethiopian distance runners (87 male, 58 female; mean age = 22.4 ± 3.1 years) using questionnaires, semi-structured interviews (n = 24), AQ1 and focus groups (n = 8).
RESULTS: Quantitative analysis revealed that, in multivariable logistic regression, primary education level (odds ratio [OR] = 5.80, q < 0.005, where q is the false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted P-value), 10th/12th certificate (OR = 0.20, q = 0.016), normal body mass index (OR = 2.85, q = 0.021), and academy training (OR = 2.40, q = 0.044) maintained statistical significance at q < 0.05, while recovery practices (OR = 2.38, q = 0.051) and centre-based training (OR = 2.23, q = 0.060) remained significant at q < 0.10. Qualitative analysis yielded three core themes: (1) The Forged Resilience: Hardship as an Unseen Training Ground; (2) The Weight of a Nation: Community as Support and Pressure; and (3) The Crossroads: Tradition Versus Modernization in Training. Integration showed that quantitative predictors were profoundly shaped by socioeconomic realities, with the "primary education" finding explained by athletes' physically demanding rural lifestyles.
CONCLUSIONS: Ethiopian distance running success is a multifaceted phenomenon embedded within a complex system of community support, organizational culture, and socioeconomic background. Sustaining success requires systemic interventions extending well beyond individual athletes to strengthen the entire ecosystem in which Ethiopian champions are made.

title: High Survival and Continued Sports Participation After Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Athletes With and Without Lateral Rim Dysplasia With Minimum 4.5-Year Follow-Up.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To quantify the outcomes, including sporting capability, of hip arthroscopy (HA) in athletes for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) in the presence of concomitant lateral rim dysplasia (LR-Dysplasia) compared with a matched athletic control group.
METHODS: Athletes undergoing unilateral primary HA for FAI with or without LR-Dysplasia between January 2009 and May 2020 were considered. All athletes with a lateral center-edge angle of <25° on anteroposterior view were matched to those with normal overcoverage (lateral center-edge angle >30°). Patients were contacted a minimum of 4.5 years after the procedure. Outcomes included survival (avoidance of total hip replacement), revision HA, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) consisting of the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity score, 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Substantial clinical benefit thresholds were determined for each PROM, and the proportion of cases achieving substantial clinical benefit was compared between groups. Finally, the ability to continue to play sports and satisfaction were determined.
RESULTS: Forty-eight patients with LR-Dysplasia were matched to 97 controls with a mean follow-up of 72 ± 19 months (54-120 months). At follow-up, survival was 100% in the LR-Dysplasia group versus 99% in controls. The revision HA rates were 6% in LR-Dysplasia patients and 9% in controls. Both groups showed significant improvements in PROMs. In the LR-Dysplasia group, mHHS improved from 82 to 100 (P < .001), UCLA from 8 to 9 (P = .114), SF-36 from 74 to 87 (P = .002), and WOMAC from 15 to 2 (P < .001). In the control group, mHHS improved from 82 to 96 (P < .001), UCLA from 7 to 10 (P = .003), SF-36 from 72 to 89 (P < .001), and WOMAC from 17 to 4 (P = .005). Between-group comparisons showed no significant differences in pre- or postoperative mHHS (P = .498; P = .183), UCLA (P = .684; P = .388), SF-36 (P = .487; P = .602), or WOMAC (P = .814; P = .390). Substantial clinical benefit was achieved by most patients for each PROM and similar between groups (P > .05 for all). No significant differences were observed between groups in PROMs or overall satisfaction with surgery (P > .05 for all). Sports participation at 5 years was 84% in the LR-Dysplasia group and 90% in controls (P = .103).
CONCLUSIONS: In the absence of arthritic changes, athletes treated with arthroscopy for FAI where LR-Dysplasia is present showed high survival rates and improved pain and function. Furthermore, most athletes can maintain their preoperative levels of sport. Importantly, the outcomes observed in this specific patient cohort are comparable to those seen in athletes with normal acetabular coverage, indicating that the presence of LR-Dysplasia does not compromise the effectiveness of arthroscopic intervention for FAI in athletes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.

title: Effect of subtendon-specific loading on strain heterogeneity in the rat Achilles tendon across gaits: A finite element study.
abstract: The Achilles tendon is comprised of three subtendons connecting to the soleus and the lateral and medial gastrocnemius muscles. These subtendons transmit load partly independently, resulting in non-uniform deformation of the tendon. Most previous computational models treating the tendon as a single homogeneous structure cannot capture the heterogeneous mechanics of the tendon. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the strain heterogeneity arising from subtendinous physiological gait loading in an anatomically detailed FE model of the rat Achilles tendon. To achieve this, phase-contrast enhanced synchrotron X-ray tomography images of rat Achilles tendons were segmented to identify the subtendon geometry and fiber distribution. Subtendon-specific experimental forces were obtained from the literature for walking, trotting, and galloping. The effect of subtendon-specific loading was investigated by comparing it to uniform loading, in which the same total force was applied to the whole proximal cross-section without distinguishing the subtendons. The resulting subtendon elongations, principal strains, shear stresses, and fluid velocities were analyzed to understand the effect of the loading scheme for various gait conditions. The results show that subtendon-specific loading substantially affected the tendon's mechanical behavior. It reproduced the differential subtendon elongation of a healthy tendon, with medial gastrocnemius elongation up to 27% higher and soleus elongation up to 29% lower than under uniform loading. Subtendinous loading also produced greater strain heterogeneity, with a maximum principal strain of 16% higher than with uniform loading, localized shear stress concentrations at the subtendon interfaces, and higher fluid velocities in the gastrocnemius compartments. Capturing these heterogeneous strain distributions is important for future mechanobiological predictions of tendon adaptation, injury, and healing.
journal: Journal of the mechanical behavior of biomedical materials

title: Altered mechanical and vascular responses of the Achilles tendon to acute loading in Kendo athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to elucidate acute, bilateral Achilles tendon (AT) responses to high-intensity single-leg hopping in Kendo athletes and healthy controls.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty Kendo athletes and 20 sedentary controls performed a single-leg hopping task. Ultrasound imaging assessed AT anteroposterior diameter (APD), shear wave velocity (SWV), and intratendinous vessel count before (PRE), immediately after (POST), and 5-min post-exercise (POST5).
RESULTS: Following exercise, Kendo athletes exhibited a significant main effect of time for both APD (P = 0.012) and SWV (P = 0.012), regardless of side. No significant acute changes in APD or SWV were observed in the control group. For intratendinous vascularity, a significant side-by-time interaction was observed in Kendo athletes (P = 0.026): the right leg showed no significant change, whereas the left leg exhibited a progressive increase from PRE to POST (P < 0.001) and further increased at POST5 (P = 0.002). In the control group, vessel count significantly increased at POST (P = 0.023) but rapidly returned to baseline. In the three-way analyses, no significant Group × Side × Time interaction was observed for any imaging outcome.
CONCLUSION: Within Kendo athletes, morphological and mechanical responses occurred bilaterally, whereas the temporal vascular response differed between the left and right Achilles tendons. However, this side-specific vascular pattern was not shown to differ significantly from that observed in sedentary controls.

title: Skeletal Muscle sEVs Mediate Exercise-Induced Cardioprotection in I/R Injury.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise training has been demonstrated to provide direct endogenous cardioprotection and to reduce cardiovascular disease risk. Skeletal muscle functions not only as an organ for movement but also as a vital secretory organ. However, how muscle-heart crosstalk contributes to exercise-induced cardioprotection remains largely unclear. Here, we investigated the cardioprotective effects of exercise-induced small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) derived from skeletal muscle in myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (MI/R) injury in mice.
METHODS: An adeno-associated virus 8-dMCK (double-muscle creatine kinase)-CD63-EGFP (enhanced green fluorescent protein) reporter system was used to track skeletal muscle-derived sEVs in the heart of mice after 4 weeks of exercise. To determine whether sEVs from exercised skeletal muscle mediate cardioprotection, cardiac sEV abundance was increased by intramyocardial injection and decreased by generating skeletal muscle-specific Rab27a knockout mice. The molecular mechanism was elucidated by profiling sEV-enriched microRNAs and validating their functions in cardiomyocytes and mouse MI/R injury models. The translational potential was then assessed in human exercise cohorts. Finally, the therapeutic efficacy was evaluated using miRNA agomirs and adeno-associated virus 8-mediated, skeletal muscle-specific overexpression of miRNAs in MI/R injury models.
RESULTS: Exercise promoted the entry of skeletal muscle-derived sEVs into the heart. Skeletal muscle-derived sEVs from exercised mice significantly attenuated MI/R injury by reducing cardiomyocyte apoptosis and improving mitochondrial respiration. Exercise-mediated protection against MI/R injury was attenuated after inhibiting the secretion of sEVs from skeletal muscle. Mechanistically, exercise-enriched sEVs delivered miR-451a and miR-143-3p to cardiomyocytes, thereby modulating the PERK (protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase)-ATF4-CHOP stress-response pathway and the USP46/P53 axis, thus reducing cardiomyocyte death. Skeletal muscle-specific overexpression of miR-451a/143-3p recapitulated the cardioprotective effects of exercise in vivo. Furthermore, exercising humans also showed elevated levels of miR-451a/143-3p in their skeletal muscle and circulating sEVs.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study reveals a novel exercise-induced cardioprotective mechanism via muscle-heart crosstalk, highlighting a promising therapeutic approach for treating cardiovascular disease.

title: Adipose-Derived Orthobiologics and Extracellular Vesicles in Foot and Ankle Surgery: Current Evidence and Clinical Limitations.
abstract: Interest in adipose-derived orthobiologics and extracellular vesicles (EVs) has expanded as clinicians seek minimally invasive treatments for musculoskeletal disorders. However, culture-expanded adipose-derived stromal cells, stromal vascular fraction, microfragmented adipose tissue (MFAT), and isolated EVs are biologically and regulatorily distinct products. This narrative review summarizes their biological rationale, processing, clinical evidence, regulatory considerations, and potential application in foot and ankle surgery. Randomized studies in knee osteoarthritis suggest that MFAT may provide symptomatic improvement, but it has not consistently demonstrated superiority over other orthobiologic injections, and the certainty of evidence remains low. Preclinical EV studies provide biological plausibility for effects on tendon healing, tendon-to-bone integration, and cartilage repair. However, substantial heterogeneity in cellular source, preparation, dose, and experimental model limits translation. Human orthopaedic EV evidence remains confined to early studies in knee osteoarthritis using placental or umbilical cord derived products, with limited and conflicting evidence of efficacy and no completed studies specific to the foot and ankle. No adipose-derived regenerative medicine or EV product is Food and Drug Administration-approved for an orthopaedic indication. Current evidence therefore does not support routine clinical use or claims of tissue regeneration. Standardized product characterization and well-designed comparative trials are required to establish safety, efficacy, and appropriate clinical applications.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Effect of Pulsed Electromagnetic Stimulation on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The effect of pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy on muscle performance and serum creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Mb) values - the biomarkers of muscle damage in experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) - has yet to be investigated. PEMF therapy is known to be effective to reduce muscle pain, muscle recovery time, fatigue but not to increase muscle force production. The study aimed to compare the effect of PEMF and sham therapy on experimentally induced DOMS in sedentary undergraduate college students.
HYPOTHESIS: PEMF therapy would improve pain, pressure pain threshold (PPT), functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration compared with the sham intervention.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, participant- and assessor-blinded, sham-controlled study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: This study was conducted at Pamukkale University Sarayköy Vocational School. A total of 52 healthy sedentary people received 3 consecutive days of active (Experimental group, n = 26) or sham (Sham group, n = 26) PEMF therapy 24 hours after DOMS induction with a drop-jump protocol. Pain intensity, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration were assessed at baseline, 24 hours and 72 hours after DOMS induction protocol.
RESULTS: The drop-jump protocol induced DOMS successfully in both groups (P < 0.05). All outcome measures were improved in the experimental group (P < 0.05). Mean change scores of PPT (P = 0.53), functional performance (P = 0.10), serum CK (P = 0.38), and Mb concentrations (P = 0.08) were not significantly different between baseline and 72 hours in the sham group. Statistically significant decreases in Mb concentrations were determined in the sham group (P = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration. The duration of PEMF therapy was sufficient to resolve the PPT, functional performance, and serum CK and Mb concentrations associated with DOMS.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study adds to existing knowledge in showing that, compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration.

title: Developmental Differences in Muscle, Tendon, and Cartilage Injuries in Elite Badminton.
abstract: This study investigated severe muscle, tendon, and cartilage injury characteristics by injury timing and post-injury management among elite badminton players. A retrospective interview study was conducted with 126 badminton players aged 19-24 years. A total of 87 severe injury cases reported by 73 athletes were analyzed, with some athletes contributing more than one case. Injuries were classified by timing into the secondary school group (SSG, n = 33) and the post-secondary group (PSG, n = 54). Injury characteristics and post-injury management were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, with effect sizes. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) examined associations with injury timing. Compared with the SSG, the PSG had higher odds of lower limb muscle injuries (OR = 6.00, 95% CI = 1.85-19.47, p = .003) and smash/stroke-related injuries (OR = 5.43, 95% CI = 1.15-25.66, p = .033), whereas the PSG had lower odds of lower limb tendinopathies (OR = 0.21, 95% CI = 0.08-0.55, p = .001). These findings suggest that severe injury characteristics may differ according to the timing of injury occurrence, despite no significant between-group differences in post-injury management, and may help inform potential injury prevention priorities based on the observed injury patterns.

title: The Impact of Tourniquet Duration on Postoperative Opioid Use and Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tourniquet use during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains common, but its effects on postoperative pain, opioid use, and stiffness are unclear. We evaluated whether tourniquet duration was associated with pain- and stiffness-related outcomes after primary TKA.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective study of 17,850 adults undergoing primary unilateral TKA at a single center from March 2016 to June 2023. Tourniquet use was categorized by inflation time relative to operative time as no tourniquet (n = 1,243), partial tourniquet (less than 0.6; n = 2,914), tourniquet-until-arthrotomy-closure (≥ 0.6 to less than 1; n = 10,003), or full-duration tourniquet (≥ 1; n = 3,690). The primary outcome was postoperative pain assessed by postoperative inpatient and cumulative 90-day morphine milligram equivalents (MME). The secondary outcomes were hours to clear physical therapy (PT), manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) within 120 days, and patient-reported Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) at six weeks. Multivariable regressions adjusted for covariates. The no-tourniquet group served as the reference.
RESULTS: Partial-tourniquet use was associated with lower 90-day opioid consumption (-90 MME; 95% confidence interval (CI) -150 to -30; P = 0.003). Tourniquet-until-closure and full-duration tourniquet were associated with higher inpatient opioid consumption (+10 MMEs; 95% CI, 2 to 17; P = 0.015; and +14 MMEs; 95% CI, 6 to 22; P = 0.001), longer time to PT clearance (+2.7 hours, 95% CI, 1.0 to 4.5; P = 0.002; and +4.1 hours, 95% CI, 2.2 to 5.9; P < 0.001), and higher adjusted odds (OR) of MUA (OR 1.78, 95% CI, 1.14 to 2.79; P = 0.012; and OR 1.64, 95% CI, 1.02 to 2.64; P = 0.040). Partial-tourniquet use was not associated with increased time to clear PT or increased odds of MUA. The KOOS JR scores did not differ significantly across strategies.
CONCLUSIONS: Tourniquet use during TKA showed duration-dependent associations with postoperative outcomes. Partial-tourniquet use may represent a balanced strategy, associated with lower cumulative 90-day opioid consumption without the delayed PT clearance or increased MUA risk observed with longer-duration tourniquet strategies.

title: Ageing increases the net metabolic cost of running alongside an ankle-to-hip redistribution of joint mechanical work.
abstract: Ageing is associated with a higher net cost of transport of running (COTnet), reduced stiffness of the Achilles tendon and a decrease in plantar flexor force. As it reduces distal propulsion capacity, the latter has been suggested as the cause of a redistribution of joint work during running, a potential cause of the increase in COTnet. Eighteen young athletes and 18 master athletes were recruited. In the first session, maximal isometric plantar flexion moment and Achilles tendon stiffness were measured; in the second, participants ran two 6 min treadmill trials at 2.5 and 3.0 m s-1, where ground reaction forces, kinematics and gas exchange were recorded to compute COTnet, joint work and Achilles tendon strain energy. Master athletes exhibited a higher COTnet than young athletes at 2.5 m s-1 (estimated marginal mean±s.e. 4.02±0.11 and 3.81±0.11 J kg-1 m-1, respectively), and this difference was greater at 3.0 m s-1 (4.29±0.12 and 3.81±0.11 J kg-1 m-1, respectively). Master athletes exhibited lower maximal isometric plantar flexor moment and, during running, lower ankle work and higher hip work. However, hip, knee and ankle work were not associated with COTnet, and Achilles tendon strain energy did not differ between groups. These findings show that the higher COTnet in master athletes coincides with a distal-to-proximal redistribution of joint work and lower Achilles tendon force, while a tendency toward lower tendon stiffness may have helped preserve tendon strain energy despite reduced loading. Whether these age-related adaptations contribute to the higher COTnet remains to be established.

title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

title: Macrophages in rotator cuff injuries and tendon-to-bone healing: Heterogeneity, pathophysiology, and therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Rotator cuff tears (RCTs) are a leading cause of shoulder disability, with high postoperative failure rates primarily attributed to poor tendon-to-bone healing. Macrophages act as central regulators of the inflammatory and regenerative microenvironment in the injured enthesis, tendon stump, subacromial bursa, and rotator cuff musculature. This review highlights the spatiotemporal heterogeneity and phenotypic plasticity of macrophages revealed by single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. Rather than following a simple M1-to-M2 transition, macrophages adopt context-dependent inflammatory, resolving, remodeling, and profibrotic programs across different stages and tissue compartments of rotator cuff injury. Persistent inflammatory programs are associated with chronic inflammation, matrix degradation, fatty infiltration, and muscle atrophy, whereas resolving and reparative programs may support inflammation resolution and fibrocartilaginous regeneration; sustained remodeling or profibrotic states may also contribute to pathological fibrosis. The review further explores macrophage-stem cell crosstalk under mechanical loading and the contribution of dysregulated macrophage function to the progression of cuff tear arthropathy. Advanced strategies including stem cell-derived exosomes, immuno-engineered scaffolds, and targeted immunomodulation, have shown therapeutic potential in preclinical studies, but their clinical efficacy and translational applicability remain to be established.

title: Five-Year Outcomes and Return to Sport After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in Young Patients With Minimal (<10%) or No Glenoid Bone Loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Arthroscopic Bankart repair is commonly used to address anterior instability in adolescents and young adults with no or minimal bone loss. However, failure rates remain high, particularly in high-risk populations.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate clinical outcomes, return-to-sport (RTS) rates, and predictors of failure after arthroscopic Bankart repair in patients ≤24 years of age with minimal glenoid bone loss. It was hypothesized that patients would demonstrate favorable outcomes, low recurrence rates, and high RTS rates, and smaller distance-to-dislocation (DTD) measurements, and contact sports participation would be associated with failure.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: The data of patients with anterior shoulder instability and minimal bone loss (<10%) who underwent primary arthroscopic Bankart repair between 2006 and 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. Remplissage was not performed. Data collected included preoperative instability events, patient-reported outcome measures, satisfaction, radiographic measurements (glenoid bone loss, glenoid track, and DTD), and RTS outcomes. Failure was defined as re-dislocation or recurrent instability requiring surgery.
RESULTS: A total of 130 patients were evaluated; 18 were excluded, leaving 112. Of these, 96 patients (85.7%) were available for the final follow-up (mean age, 19.9 ± 3.1 years; mean follow-up, 68.4 ± 42.7 months). All clinical outcomes improved significantly (P < .05) except for the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey Mental Component Summary score. The median satisfaction score was 9 (IQR, 8-10). Participation in contact sports was associated with failure, while other risk factors were not. RTS was achieved by 96.1% of patients; however, only 57.1% returned to their preinjury level. Fewer preoperative dislocation events were associated with successful return to full activity (P = .04). The recurrence rate was 33.3%, and revision surgery was required in 19 patients (19.8%).
CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic Bankart repair was associated with high rates of recurrence and revision surgery in a series of patients ≤24 years of age without glenoid bone loss. In those who did not require revision surgery, clinical outcomes and RTS rates were high. Contact sports participation was associated with failure. A greater number of preoperative instability events negatively influence RTS outcomes. Arthroscopic Bankart repair in this population is safe and has a low complication rate, but the failure rate remains considerable.

title: The Applied Sport Science of Professional Male Basketball: A Narrative Review of Current and Emerging Practices.
abstract: Basketball is a physically demanding intermittent team sport which requires a multifaceted approach to optimise player preparation, performance, health, and recovery. Quantifying the training and match demands of professional basketball players can help practitioners develop effective strategies for managing fatigue, monitoring training loads, and guiding physical preparation. Sleep and travel disruptions present additional challenges to practitioners and can have deleterious effects on recovery and readiness to compete. Nutrition is also an essential component supporting performance and recovery and should be individualised to the needs of each player. The inherent complexity of basketball requires practitioners to develop a holistic view that considers the interaction between tactical, technical, psychological, and physical basketball-related factors along with external factors from the greater basketball system (e.g., players, coaches, support staff, organisations, schedules, referees, and governing bodies) that can influence performance. Advances in technology continue to shape performance monitoring, injury-risk forecasting, and training methodologies, yet practitioners must be aware of potential risks such as player privacy concerns and the misuse of data. A comprehensive understanding of these factors provides valuable insights for practitioners to develop effective evidence-based strategies and frameworks for working with professional male basketball players.

title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: High-Strength Tape for Cable Structure Reconstruction During Arthroscopic Repair of L-Shaped Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract: With the innovation and progressive maturation of arthroscopic techniques, the advantages of minimally invasive surgery and accelerated rehabilitation have made arthroscopy a preferred option for patients with rotator cuff injuries. However, for complex rotator cuff tears, such as "L-shaped" tendon tears, the risk of postoperative retear remains considerable. The cable structure, serving as a "suspension bridge" within the rotator cuff, is a critical load-bearing component of the shoulder joint. This structure is frequently compromised in "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. In this report, we describe an arthroscopic technique using high-strength tape to restore the cable structure and treat "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. The key steps include using high-strength tape to reduce the retracted tendon stump and restore the cable structure, thereby re-establishing mechanical integrity, reducing tension on the repaired tendon, and minimizing the cutting effect of sutures on the tendon. Finally, the sutures from the medial-row anchor are employed to perform a "Margin Convergence" repair of the longitudinal tear component.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.
