title: Autism spectrum disorder and mild traumatic brain injury in the pediatric population: a scoping review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Concussions (i.e., mild traumatic brain injuries [mTBIs]) commonly produce transient neurocognitive and somatic symptoms that may overlap with baseline characteristics of neurodiverse populations. The relationship between autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and concussion/mTBI remains poorly characterized. This scoping review sought to synthesize existing literature evaluating concussion/mTBI risk, baseline neurocognitive testing, and symptom reporting in individuals with ASD.
METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Embase, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and CENTRAL databases were searched for studies evaluating ASD and concussion or mTBI. The central research question was the following: What is the current state of knowledge related to concussions/mTBI in patients with ASD? This review sought to evaluate the areas of baseline testing, acute symptomatology, injury characteristics, and recovery. Studies were required to explicitly evaluate ASD in relation to concussion/mTBI outcomes or neurocognitive testing. Studies that did not isolate ASD from other neurodevelopmental disorders, as well as reviews, editorials, and conference abstracts, were excluded.
RESULTS: The search identified 374 studies, of which 7 (1.9%) met full inclusion criteria after screening. Most studies evaluated baseline neurocognitive testing using the Immediate Post-Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT) platform in pediatric/adolescent athletes. Three studies (42.9%) reported that individuals with ASD were more likely to produce invalid baseline neurocognitive scores and demonstrated differences in certain cognitive composites compared with controls. Two studies (28.6%) evaluated baseline concussion-like symptoms, with one reporting higher symptom endorsement among athletes with ASD and the other finding no statistically significant differences from controls. Epidemiological studies did not demonstrate a clear association between ASD and increased risk of concussion. Notably, no identified studies evaluated acute postinjury symptom trajectories or recovery outcomes following concussion in individuals with ASD.
CONCLUSIONS: Existing literature examining ASD and concussion/TBI primarily evaluated baseline neurocognitive testing and suggested potential differences in testing performance and symptom reporting among individuals with ASD. However, the authors identified a critical lack of studies evaluating acute symptoms and recovery trajectories following concussion/mTBI in this population, which represents a significant barrier for clinicians-from athletic trainers to pediatricians to pediatric neurosurgeons-in accurately diagnosing, risk stratifying, and managing these patients in the postinjury setting. Prospective investigations are needed to better define concussion/mTBI presentation, recovery patterns, and optimal management strategies for individuals with ASD.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: More than a shot: function over pain with tele-supervised resistance exercise added to hyaluronic acid injection in knee osteoarthritis, a randomized add-on trial.
abstract: Exercise is central to knee osteoarthritis (KOA) care, and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (IAHA) is often used as an adjunct, yet access to supervised exercise after injection is limited. Whether adding tele-supervised resistance band exercise (TSBE) improves outcomes beyond IAHA alone is unclear. Eighty adults with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 1-3 KOA who had not responded adequately to conservative care received a single IAHA injection and were allocated to a 12-week TSBE or standard education without supervised exercise. The between-group difference in Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total change favoured TSBE (-5 points, 95% CI - 9.86 to -0.13; p = .044). TSBE also favoured WOMAC physical function (-4.88, 95% CI - 8.28 to -1.47), 30-second sit-to-stand (+3.79 repetitions, 95% CI 2.80 to 4.79), and timed up-and-go (-1.87 s, 95% CI - 2.34 to -1.41), but not VAS pain (-0.38, 95% CI - 1.00 to 0.25). Adding TSBE to IAHA improved function and mobility, with no additional reduction in pain.

title: Spatial transcriptomics in immune-mediated necrotising myopathy uncovers a specific necrotic signature related to immune-driven fibrosis.
abstract: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathies (IMNM) are characterised by muscle fibre necrosis, complement deposits around non-necrotic fibres, and macrophage infiltrates. Patients experience muscle damage with fibro-fatty replacement, leading to poor strength recovery, but the pathogenesis remains unclear. To investigate IMNM pathogenesis, we applied spatial transcriptomics on myositis muscle biopsies and integrated the results with published single-nucleus transcriptomic data. This combined approach enabled analysis of gene expression with spatial localisation in the muscle. Inflammatory, fibrotic, regenerative, and lipid metabolism-related signatures were identified in IMNM, distinct from other myositis, with specific distribution in necrotic and peri-necrotic regions. A unique subtype of immune-driven fibroblasts expressing SFRP4 was enriched in IMNM necrotic areas. These cells carried a strong proportion of IMNM-enriched pathological signatures, notably a complement-linked 'tumour-like' inflammatory fibroblast signature and a specific interferon response, characterised by the expression of metallothioneins. Peri-necrotic areas were characterised by pathological muscle signatures carrying interferon response and FABP4+ metabolically dysfunctional signatures. In conclusion, IMNM necrotic muscle areas are linked to a specific SFRP4-expressing fibroblast subtype interacting with macrophages, potentially driving the pathological muscle phenotype and contributing to inflammation, fibro-fatty replacement, and strength loss.

title: Statistical Parametric Mapping reveals sex-specific, phase-dependent differences in bilateral three-dimensional ground reaction force during Wushu Changbing PiJi in high-level athletes.
abstract: PiJi is a core attacking technique in Wushu Changbing competition, but continuous waveform evidence remains limited regarding the sex-specific phase characteristics of bilateral 3D ground reaction force (GRF) during PiJi performed with maximal voluntary effort (MVE). This study aimed to compare continuous changes in trailing-foot, lead-foot, and net bilateral GRF between high-level male and female athletes during PiJi performed with MVE. In this cross-sectional, laboratory-based observational study, 44 right-hand-dominant athletes, including 22 male athletes and 22 female athletes, performed PiJi with MVE, yielding 616 valid trials. Bilateral 3D GRF was recorded using two force plates. Each trial was time-normalized and linearly interpolated to 143 equally spaced nodes, and within-participant mean waveforms were calculated before between-group differences were analyzed using statistical parametric mapping. Primary analyses used random-field-theory inference, with sensitivity examined using 5,000 permutation tests. After Bonferroni correction, phase-specific sex differences were detected in trailing-foot, lead-foot, and net bilateral 3D GRF. Scalar localization showed that male athletes had higher trailing-foot Fy during the middle phase (33.98%-47.04%) and higher trailing-foot Fx (62.41%-71.99%) and net bilateral Fx (54.18%-70.41%) during the middle-to-late phase; female athletes showed only a brief period of higher trailing-foot vertical Fz during the middle phase (42.11%-44.61%). Although lead-foot 3D GRF differed overall, no confirmatory difference was localized to any single scalar component. These findings indicate that sex-related GRF differences in high-level PiJi were concentrated mainly in specific horizontal-plane phases of trailing-foot and net bilateral force, whereas the lead-foot difference was identified only at the overall 3D GRF level. These results provide kinetic evidence for phase-specific assessment of PiJi technique and suggest that training monitoring and mechanistic research should consider foot, direction, and movement phase rather than relying only on peak force or discrete variables. Future studies integrating multimodal measures and sport-specific performance may further clarify the functional significance of bilateral force-generation patterns.

title: Multimodal rehabilitation interventions reduce pain in dogs with osteoarthritis, regardless of enrollment in formal in-clinic or outpatient rehabilitation.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The objective was to determine the effects of multimodal rehabilitation interventions on Canine Brief Pain Inventory (CBPI) pain scores in dogs diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA), and to determine whether effects differed between formal in-clinic versus outpatient rehabilitation.
ANIMALS AND PROCEDURE: Medical records from between 2022 and 2024 were reviewed for dogs with OA that were presented to a rehabilitation specialist. Each dog's caregiver completed a CBPI at both the initial evaluation and 1st follow-up visit. Dogs were allocated into 2 groups: those that received in-clinic rehabilitation and those that received outpatient interventions. Both groups received customized, multimodal plans to address their OA signs. Pain severity scores (PSS), pain interference scores (PIS), and overall interference scores were compared between groups. A 2-sample Student's t-test or a Fisher's exact test was used to compare groups, with a statistical significance level of 0.05.
RESULTS: A total of 79 dogs were included in the study. There were no differences between dogs enrolled in in-clinic rehabilitation versus outpatient rehabilitation for sex, age, weight, or body condition score (P = 0.541, P = 0.26, P = 0.58, P = 0.33, respectively). The PSS and PIS had improved at the 1st recheck in both groups (in-clinic: P = 0.01 and P = 0.03; outpatient: P = 0.03 and P = 0.03, respectively).
CONCLUSION AND CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Owner-perceived pain decreased in all dogs, whether they were enrolled in formal in-clinic rehabilitation or not. This was attributed to customized interventions, including rehabilitation, pain management, and weight management. Our results corroborated reports that multimodal OA management plans, including rehabilitation interventions, ameliorate symptoms of OA in humans. Given the high prevalence of canine OA, this study supported the beneficial effects of multimodal rehabilitation interventions on the well-being of osteoarthritic dogs.

title: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders among civil servants attending healthcare facilities in Bangladesh: An observational cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a major occupational health concern worldwide, significantly affecting employees' well-being and productivity. Government employees in Bangladesh are particularly vulnerable to WMSDs due to the sedentary or repetitive nature of their work (e.g., prolonged computer use, repetitive typing, and manual mechanical tasks).ObjectiveThis study aimed to determine the clinical distribution, patterns, and associated factors of WMSDs among government employees in Bangladesh and evaluate the subjective impact on workers' productivity and quality of life.MethodsA retrospective descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted at the Government Employees Hospital in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Participants were recruited using consecutive sampling from government employees attending the Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation Department. Descriptive and inferential statistics (Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests via R software) were used to examine the distribution of conditions like low back pain, knee osteoarthritis, cervical spondylosis, frozen shoulder. Productivity and quality of life were assessed through structured clinical interviews, while demographic characteristics, work type, and employment grade were analyzed to identify associated factors.ResultsNonspecific low back pain was the most prevalent condition (27.23%), particularly among retired employees (34.62%) and sedentary workers (26.97%). Knee osteoarthritis (10.81%) and cervical spondylosis (8.97%) were more common among older and dynamic workers. The most commonly affected sites were the lower back (43.73%), knees, shoulders, and neck. Disease patterns varied significantly by age, and government service grade.ConclusionThe high proportion of diagnosed cases among Bangladeshi government employees underscores the need for interventions including ergonomic modifications, regular health assessments, and early screening strategies to reduce WMSD impact and inform public sector health policies.

title: Adipose-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells: Isolation, Origin, Phenotype Applications, and Challenges.
abstract: Traditional adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (AD-MSCs) research has relied on unfractionated bulk populations, whose therapeutic efficacy is constrained by cellular heterogeneity, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and rapid postengraftment functional exhaustion, resulting in inconsistent outcomes and impeding clinical translation. This review systematically examines AD-MSC developmental origins, tissue niches, isolation and purification strategies, functional phenotypes, and biomanufacturing bottlenecks. It integrates preclinical and clinical evidence for AD-MSCs and their extracellular vesicles (EVs) in bone and cartilage regeneration, chronic cutaneous diseases, neurological disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and other conditions. These therapies remodel injured microenvironments through immunometabolic reprogramming, antifibrotic signaling, angiogenesis, mitochondrial transfer, and paracrine regulation rather than direct tissue replacement. Major translational barriers include cellular heterogeneity, safety concerns, the transdifferentiation controversy, nonstandardized preconditioning, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and low cell retention after transplantation. We propose that clinical translation should be based on prospective isolation of functional subpopulations, coupled with tailored preconditioning, precision gene editing, three-dimensional biomaterials, EV engineering, and automated closed-system biomanufacturing. This framework aims to preserve potency, phenotypic stability, and paracrine function, transforming AD-MSCs and their bioactive derivatives from variable, unfractionated preparations into well-characterized, standardized, highly potent precision biologics. More broadly, it offers a mechanism-driven, function-defined, engineering-enabled, and clinically accessible roadmap for next-generation regenerative medicine.

title: Progression of peak athletic performance age in the past four decades.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Older athletes are redefining the prime by extending their athletic longevity. A trend that women's peak performance age tends to increase, while men's remains largely unchanged, has been reported some time ago. The present study builds on this early work by examining more recent data to determine whether such gender differences persisted across contemporary periods and in different sporting events.
METHODS: Ages of Olympic medalists from 1984 to 2024 were analyzed as indicators of peak performance age (N.=2016).
RESULTS: In men, peak performance ages ranged 26±2 to 28±2 years in endurance, 26±2 to 27±2 years in power, 23±1 to 24±2 years in sprint, and 26±2 to 27±2 years in skill. In women, the ranges were from 27±2 to 29±2 years for endurance, 26±2 to 28±2 years for power, 23±2 to 24±2 years for sprint, and 23±3 to 26±3 years for skill. There were no gender differences in peak performance age among endurance, power, and sprint events in any era. However, in skill sports, male athletes demonstrated a higher peak performance age in 1984-1996 (P<0.05), a difference that has since disappeared. The age variabilities show an upward trend over time in both men and women.
CONCLUSIONS: We concluded that in recent years, both male and female athletes have achieved peak performance at comparable ages across all sport types.

title: Post-COVID-19 Penalty Trends Following an Injury-Prevention Rule Change in Rhode Island High School Boys' Hockey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Penalty infraction minute (PIM)-based rule modifications have been implemented in youth and high school ice hockey to reduce injury risk. A prior Rhode Island Interscholastic League (RIIL) study demonstrated a reduction in game-related injuries following implementation of a statewide 2015-2016 50/70 PIM rule. The durability of these behavioral trends post-COVID-19 has not been evaluated.
PURPOSE: This descriptive epidemiologic study evaluates post-pandemic trends in penalty infraction minutes and disqualifying penalties in RIIL boys' varsity ice hockey.
METHODS: Publicly available RIIL varsity boys' ice hockey data were reviewed for four consecutive seasons (2021-2022 through 2024-2025). Extracted variables included total rostered players, counts of players exceeding PIM thresholds (≥25, ≥50, ≥70), mean team PIM per game, goals scored, number of participating teams, and total disqualifying penalties per season. Data were summarized descriptively by season.
RESULTS: Across four seasons, rostered players ranged from 479 to 540, with 21 to 25 teams competing annually. Mean team PIM per game remained stable, ranging from 8.13 to 8.83. No players accumulated ≥50 or ≥70 PIM in any season. Players accumulating ≥25 PIM ranged from 17 to 24 per season. Disqualifying penalties occurred each season (range, 5-11 per year) without a consistent directional trend. Goals scored remained proportional to participating teams.
CONCLUSIONS: In post-pandemic seasons, PIM distributions and disqualifying penalties remained stable, with no recurrence of high-PIM accumulations requiring suspension. These findings suggest sustained behavioral patterns following rule modifications, but cannot be interpreted as evidence of injury reduction without injury surveillance data. Continued monitoring incorporating injury outcomes is warranted.

title: Initial Acceleration Deficit as a Timing-Derived Performance Metric of Early-Phase Sprint Acceleration in Elite Youth Soccer Players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To examine the applied relevance of initial acceleration deficit (IAD) as a timing-derived performance metric of early-phase sprint acceleration in elite youth soccer players.
METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 112 elite male youth soccer players (aged 15-18 y). Sprint performance was assessed over 25 m using dual-beam timing gates (splits at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 m). IAD was calculated as the difference between the 0- to 10- and 5- to 15-m intervals derived from the same trial. Vertical jump performance and anthropometric characteristics were also assessed. IAD was additionally expressed in normalized form, and percentile-based reference values (25th, 50th, and 75th) were established.
RESULTS: A strong association was observed between IAD and 0- to 10-m sprint time (r = .805, P < .001). No significant associations were observed between IAD and vertical jump performance or anthropometric variables (all P > .10), whereas 20-m sprint time demonstrated moderate associations with jump performance. No significant positional differences were identified for IAD; however, goalkeepers exhibited a nonsignificant tendency for faster 0- to 10-m times without corresponding differences in IAD.
CONCLUSION: IAD represents a timing-derived performance metric of early acceleration structure. While derived from shared temporal components with sprint time, it provides additional insight into how acceleration is distributed during the initial phase of sprinting. Expression in normalized form may support athlete profiling and monitoring in applied environments where advanced biomechanical assessment is not feasible.

title: Aerobic exercise preconditioning enhances skeletal muscle resistance and recovery after contusion: involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Compared with passive recovery after injury, exercise preconditioning may provide an active strategy for improving the subsequent response of skeletal muscle to injury. This study aimed to investigate the effects of aerobic exercise preconditioning (AEP) on skeletal muscle injury (SMI) and post-injury repair, with particular focus on the involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and changes in PGC-1α acetylation.
METHODS: This study initially investigated the effects of continuous aerobic exercise on skeletal muscle in healthy mice. Subsequently, the influence of AEP on injury severity and regenerative repair of the gastrocnemius muscle was examined in mice with SMI. Western blotting was used to determine the expression levels of SIRT1 and PGC-1α proteins, immunoprecipitation was performed to assess the acetylation status of PGC-1α, and qRT-PCR was used to analyze the expression of genes associated with mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers and muscle regeneration. Finally, the involvement of SIRT1 signaling in the AEP-associated response to SMI was further examined using the pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor EX527.
RESULTS: Continuous aerobic exercise was associated with increased SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling and changes in mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers in the gastrocnemius muscle of healthy mice. AEP was associated with reduced injury-related changes and an improved post-injury repair profile in mice with SMI. During the early stage after injury, AEP was accompanied by sustained SIRT1/ PGC-1α signaling and reduced PGC-1α acetylation. Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 with EX527 partially attenuated the AEP-associated protective and reparative effects on the injured gastrocnemius muscle.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that AEP establishes an adaptive state in skeletal muscle that is associated with reduced injury-related damage and an enhanced post-injury reparative response. The SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and altered PGC-1α acetylation may contribute to these AEP-associated effects.

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

title: Dynamics of Sleep Architecture and Nocturnal Oxygen Saturation During Acclimatization at Intermediate Altitude: A Longitudinal Observational Study in Elite Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletes typically undergo training camps living and sleeping at intermediate altitudes (1500-2500 m). Hypoxia reshapes sleep through central circuits regulating arousal, chemoreflex gain and sympathetic outflow. However, the relationship between peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and sleep architecture and how it co-evolves during acclimatization, is unclear.
METHODS: We tested whether SpO2 differs across sleep stages at intermediate altitude and whether its recovery is stage specific. Seventeen mogul-ski athletes (seven women) travelled from Montréal (Canada) to Tignes (France) for a 2-week altitude training camp (AltitudeCamp; 2100 m) in June 2025. During the first week (6 nights) and the last night of AltitudeCamp, athletes were provided with a validated ring pulse oximeter and an electroencephalography (EEG) headband. We evaluated the changes in sleep stage distribution across successive nights, scored on 30-second epochs and synchronized with oximetry data. Model estimates are reported as mean ± Standard Error (SE), raw data as mean ± Standard Deviation (SD).
RESULTS: Average total sleep time was 429 ± 47 min (mean ± SD) and did not change during AltitudeCamp (p = 0.939). Across the first week, %N3 decreased logarithmically (β = -2.35 ± 0.72%/ln (night), p = 0.002) and %Rapid eye movement sleep (REM) increased logarithmically (β = 3.13 ± 0.88%/ln (night), p < 0.001), with no changes in %Wake, %N1, or %N2. SpO2 was lower during AltitudeCamp (95.2 ± 0.3%) than measures obtained in normoxia (98 ± 0.4%; p < 0.001), and overnight heart rate (HR) was 7 ± 2 beats per minute (bpm) higher than the habitual 58 ± 3 bpm observed in normoxia (p = 0.005). Wake SpO2 increased by 0.13 ± 0.01 percentage points per night (p < 0.001), with faster recovery in N1 (0.19 ± 0.02 percentage points/night; p = 0.006) and REM (0.23 ± 0.01 percentage points/night; p < 0.001), while N2 and N3 did not differ from Wake. HR declined by 0.79 bpm/night during Wake, similar to N3 (p = 0.26), but larger than the decline in N1 (p = 0.024) and REM (p < 0.001). In N2, HR did not evolve during the first week at altitude.
CONCLUSIONS: At intermediate altitude, nocturnal SpO2 and HR show sleep-stage-specific dynamics that mirror central ventilatory and autonomic adaptation to hypoxia. Our data suggest that acclimatization is not uniform across sleep stages, and that the first 2 nights after ascent may capture the most rapid adjustments despite similar total sleep duration. Sleep therefore offers a heterogeneous and ecologically valid index of central nervous system (CNS) acclimatization, which can be monitored longitudinally with wearable EEG-oximetry.

title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

title: Atypical Suprasyndesmotic Distal Fibular Fracture in an Adolescent Athlete with Minimal Symptoms: A Case Report.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Fractures of the distal fibula are common injuries in adolescent athletes, usually associated with identifiable trauma and rapid, uneventful healing. However, atypical mechanisms and minimal symptoms may obscure the diagnosis. We aim to describe the clinical course, imaging findings, and management of a suprasyndesmotic distal fibular fracture sustained during football practice, characterized by an unusual fracture mechanism without direct contact or major trauma and minimal clinical symptoms.
CASE REPORT: We present the case of a 15-year-old male admitted to the emergency department after an injury to the left leg while at a football practice. He reported missing the ball while attempting a shot and immediately perceived a crack in the kicking leg, without any collision or contact with another player. Clinical examination revealed painless palpation of both malleoli, varus stress testing, and isolated tenderness at the distal third of the fibula, without spontaneous pain.Radiographs confirmed a fracture located between the middle and distal thirds of the fibula, compatible with a suprasyndesmotic Weber C pattern. The lesion was non-displaced and initially described as a greenstick-type fracture. Conservative treatment with a plaster splint and non-weight-bearing was initiated. No analgesics were required.
CONCLUSION: Distal fibular fractures in young athletes may occur through unusual, contactless mechanisms with minimal symptoms, even in a suprasyndesmotic Weber C fracture pattern. Clinical assessment must remain the cornerstone of decision-making, while complementary imaging is useful to rule out complications, such as pseudarthrosis. Conservative management allowed full and safe return to sport in this patient after 4 months.

title: Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes Preserve Cartilage Homeostasis and Restore Joint Function in Experimental Osteoarthritis.
abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have shown therapeutic potential for osteoarthritis (OA), but their clinical application is limited by the need for extensive ex vivo expansion. Human umbilical cord MSC-derived exosomes (hUCMSC-Exos) have emerged as a promising cell-free alternative because of their cartilage-protective and immunomodulatory properties. hUCMSC-Exos were characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis and evaluated in an interleukin-1β (IL-1β)-stimulated human chondrocyte model and an anterior cruciate ligament transection (ACLT)-induced rat OA model. In vitro, hUCMSC-Exos suppressed inflammatory and catabolic responses while enhancing extracellular matrix synthesis, as evidenced by reduced IL-1β, MMP13, and Type X collagen expression and increased TIMP1, aggrecan, and Type II collagen expression. In vivo, repeated intra-articular administration of hUCMSC-Exos attenuated cartilage degeneration, resulting in improved gross joint morphology, reduced histopathological damage, increased glycosaminoglycan deposition and Type II collagen expression, and decreased MMP13 expression. These structural improvements were accompanied by enhanced functional recovery, as demonstrated by improved hind limb weight-bearing and treadmill running endurance. These findings suggest that hUCMSC-Exos alleviate cartilage degeneration and improve joint function, supporting their potential as a promising cell-free therapeutic approach for OA.

title: All-Inside Posterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Achilles Allograft and Suture Tape Augmentation.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) reconstruction is challenged by graft elongation and delayed biological integration, often necessitating slow rehabilitation and carrying a risk of arthrofibrosis. This technical report describes an all-inside technique augmented with the modified internal bracing to address these limitations. The technique involves integrating a FiberTape within a quadrupled Achilles tendon allograft, creating a load-sharing composite. An all-inside, retrograde socket method was used for anatomic PCL reconstruction in the knee, with suspensory fixation on both femur and tibia. The graft-tape construct was simultaneously tensioned. The technique provides immediate biomechanical stability by mitigating graft micromotion, elongation, and tunnel abrasion. By closely replicating native PCL stiffness, this construct facilitates an accelerated, protective rehabilitation protocol focused on early motion and quadriceps activation, thereby aiming to reduce failure rates and postoperative stiffness. This method represents a synergistic evolution in PCL reconstruction, combining synthetic reinforcement with biological healing.

title: Flexible and stretchable bioelectronics for sports wearable monitoring: Materials, Device Engineering, and Intelligent Wearable Platforms.
abstract: Modern sports science is undergoing a paradigm shift from subjective coaching to objective, data-driven precision training. Consequently, wearable electronics for acquiring precise data during sports activities are attracting attention. However, conventional rigid wearables inherently suffer from mechanical mismatches between rigid wearables and the soft, deformable human skin, inducing severe motion artifacts and restricting natural biomechanics during high-intensity athletic activities. To address these limitations from a comprehensive perspective, this review systematically summarizes and analyzes recent advancements in next-generation flexible and stretchable bioelectronics tailored specifically for sports applications. We systematically examine the substrate materials, structural engineering designs, and device-level optimization strategies required to withstand repetitive strain, shear, and sweat-intensive environments. Building upon these conformable bio-interfaces, we discuss three core sensing modalities: electrochemical sensors for real-time analysis of sweat biomarkers, biophysical sensors for continuous electrophysiological and hemodynamic monitoring, and electromechanical sensors for high-fidelity kinematic and impact tracking. Furthermore, we discuss body-derived energy harvesting strategies to power sports wearables and wireless communication systems for continuous athletic monitoring. The importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning is increasing, as these techniques enable the removal of motion artifacts and facilitate objective analysis of athletic data for training and health monitoring applications. By evaluating targeted applications across aerobic and anaerobic exercise, cognitive state assessment, and post-exercise recovery, this review demonstrates how next-generation sports wearables contribute to the shift in sports science from reactive treatment toward proactive, data-driven performance enhancement and injury prevention.

title: Pre-season friendly match-play as a double-edged sword: Performance gains and inflammatory cost in semi-professional soccer players (a natural experiment).
abstract: Pre-season training prepares soccer players for competition, but the longitudinal effects of friendly match exposure remain unclear. We investigated whether cumulative late pre-season match-play is associated with physiological adaptation in semi-professional players. Twenty-four male players from a randomly selected semi-professional team competing at national level were assessed at pre-season start, mid-pre-season and pre-competition. Measurements included body composition, physical performance, aerobic fitness and blood markers reflecting muscle damage, inflammation, hormonal status and haematological adaptation. Based on cumulative playing time across eight friendly matches, as determined by coaching staff, players were classified retrospectively into extended play (EP) or limited play (LP) groups. Controlling for mid-pre-season baseline, the EP group showed significantly lower pre-competition values for body mass ( η p 2 = 0.276), body fat ( η p 2 = 0.294) and 35 m sprint time ( η p 2 = 0.129) and higher values for lower-limb power (dominant/non-dominant; η p 2 = 0.219-0.424), velocity at maximal oxygen uptake ( η p 2 = 0.441) and at second ventilatory threshold ( η p 2 = 0.708), serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase ( η p 2 = 0.296), myoglobin ( η p 2 = 0.199), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein ( η p 2 = 0.920), interleukin-6 ( η p 2 = 0.893), tumour necrosis factor-α ( η p 2 = 0.937) and red blood cell count ( η p 2 = 0.190) (all P ≤ 0.038). Across all participants, total match-play time was correlated significantly with reductions in body fat (r = -0.47) and increases in lower-limb power (r = 0.44-0.67), second ventilatory threshold (r = 0.55) and inflammatory markers (r = 0.79-0.86) (all P ≤ 0.033). Greater friendly match-play exposure during pre-season was associated with favourable physiological adaptations and a more pronounced physiological and inflammatory response. These findings support friendly match-play as a meaningful physiological stimulus and highlight the importance of balancing match exposure with recovery during pre-season preparation.

title: Selective Electrical Muscle Stimulation of the Vastus Medialis in a Patient With Knee Osteoarthritis, With Changes in Muscle Quality, Symptoms, and Physical Activity: A Case Report.
abstract: BACKGROUND Fat accumulation in the vastus medialis has been associated with the progression of knee osteoarthritis. Electrical muscle stimulation may reduce intramuscular fat accumulation by inducing contractions of the targeted muscle. We hypothesized that electrical stimulation of the vastus medialis would be associated with a reduction in intramuscular fat and improvement in self-reported symptoms during the observation period in a patient with knee osteoarthritis. CASE REPORT The patient was a 77-year-old man with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2 right knee osteoarthritis. Because he also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia, he had maintained regular exercise habits, including aquatic walking; however, he discontinued these activities because of knee pain. Electrical stimulation was applied to the vastus medialis for 30 minutes per session, 3 times per week, for 4 weeks. Ultrasound echo intensity, an indirect indicator of intramuscular fat, and the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score were assessed before and after the intervention. Compared with the pre-intervention value, vastus medialis echo intensity decreased by 13.7 arbitrary units (25.3%), and knee symptoms improved during the observation period. He resumed aquatic walking 2 weeks after electrical stimulation was initiated. CONCLUSIONS During the observation period, vastus medialis echo intensity decreased, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score scores improved, and he resumed aquatic walking. However, because this was a single uncontrolled case and physical activity resumed during the intervention, these changes cannot be attributed to electrical stimulation alone; spontaneous improvement, behavioral reactivation, or a combination of these factors remain plausible. Controlled studies across different levels of disease severity are needed.

title: A Six-Day High-Intensity Interval Training Microcycle Improves Selected Indicators of Endurance Performance in Well-Trained Female Cross-Country Skiers and Biathletes.
abstract: We compared the effects of a 6-day high-intensity interval training (HIT) microcycle followed by a 5-day active recovery period (HITblock) with a time-matched period of continued regular training (REG) on endurance performance in well-trained female cross-country skiers and biathletes. Seventeen athletes (maximal oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 max ): 55.1 (5.2) mL·min-1 kg-1) were assigned to either HITblock or REG. No differences in training volume or intensity were observed between the groups during the 4 weeks preceding the intervention. During the intervention, HITblock completed five HIT sessions over 6 days (6 × 5-min work intervals; target rate of perceived exertion:17-18), with increased HIT replacing part of their habitual training and thereby reducing overall training load, whereas REG continued habitual training, including 3-4 moderate- or high-intensity interval sessions. Endurance performance was assessed during roller ski skating and included 15-min time-trial average velocity (velocity15-min), velocity at 4 mmol·L-1 blood lactate (velocity4mmol), and velocity during the final minute of incremental V ˙ O 2 max testing ( velocity V ˙ O 2 max ). HITblock demonstrated greater improvements than REG in velocity V ˙ O 2 max (3.6 (2.1)% versus 1.2 (1.6)%, p = 0.024) and velocity4mmol (4.4 (2.9)% versus 0.0 (4.4)%, p = 0.023), whereas changes in velocity15-min did not differ between groups (5.4 (5.0)% versus 1.3 (3.4)%, p = 0.083). An exploratory composite performance index combining these outcomes demonstrated superior improvements in HITblock compared with REG (4.5 (2.8)% versus 0.9 (2.6)%, p = 0.017). These findings indicate that a 6-day HIT microcycle followed by a 5-day active recovery period is associated with greater improvements in selected endurance performance indicators compared with continued regular training in well-trained female cross-country skiers and biathletes.

title: Gender Differences in Sports Injuries of the Foot and Ankle.
abstract: This article examines sex-based differences in foot and ankle injuries among female athletes, emphasizing the role of anatomic, hormonal, biomechanical, and sociocultural factors. Female athletes are disproportionately affected by ankle sprains, chronic instability, and bone stress injuries. Conditions such as relative energy deficiency in sport and the female athlete triad contribute to injury risk and long-term health consequences but remain under-recognized. This article highlights disparities in research, treatment, and outcomes, calling for improved screening, sex-specific prevention strategies, and greater inclusion of female subjects in sports medicine research to inform evidence-based care and optimize outcomes for female athletes.

title: Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery: Are Marathon and Trail Running Different?
abstract: Although trail and road are two running disciplines, they have distinct characteristics potentially leading to different physiological impacts that have never been examined. The aim of the present study was to compare neuromuscular fatigue and recovery between a marathon and two trail runs of equivalent effort (29 km; ± 1,400 m). Forty-one trained runners, specialized in either road or trail running, performed a simulated treadmill marathon (MARASIM), a simulated treadmill trail run (TRAILSIM), or a trail run in natural conditions (TRAILNAT), depending on their speciality. Neuromuscular fatigue, i.e. changes in maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), voluntary activation (VA) and peak twitch (Tw) of the knee extensors (KE) and plantar flexors (PF), blood markers of muscle damage, jump performance, and force-velocity profile (FVP) were assessed before (PRE), immediately after (POST), one (+1 day), two (+2 days), and seven days (+7 days) following the runs. Muscle pain questionnaires were administered at PRE and during the month following the run. MARASIM showed significantly greater decreases in KE VA (-23.5% vs. -9.2% vs. -13.0%) and jump height (-11.7%; +11.4%; +5.9%, for squat jump), and significantly higher increases in blood markers of muscle damage (+1,726 UI.L -1; +641 UI.L -1; +363 UI.L -1; at +1 day) compared to TRAILSIM and TRAILNAT, respectively. The return to baseline occurred later in MARASIM for KE VA and jump height. Muscle soreness values also returned to baseline earlier in TRAILNAT and TRAILSIM compared to MARASIM. No differences between groups existed in KE Pt and MVC, in any PF neuromuscular fatigue variables, and FVP. Overall, marathon running appears to induce greater acute neuromuscular alterations than trail running, mostly on KE, with a slower return to baseline values.

title: Application of FTIR to detect changes in blood plasma during a pre-competition period in a professional heavyweight boxer.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES AND DESIGN: This exploratory single-case study examined whether repeated attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy of blood plasma is technically feasible during a short pre-competition period and whether spectral regions co-vary with conventionally assayed biochemical markers.
METHODS: One professional heavyweight boxer was monitored over a 13-day pre-competition period characterized by reduced training load (tapering). Morning fasting blood was collected on five occasions (10, 13, 17, 20, and 23 May 2024) into lithium-heparin tubes and centrifuged to obtain plasma. Creatine kinase (CK), C-reactive protein (CRP), glucose, cortisol, testosterone, total and reduced glutathione, malondialdehyde, and zinc were quantified by conventional laboratory assays; ATR-FTIR spectra were acquired separately from the same plasma aliquots and were not used to quantify any of these analytes. Each plasma sample was measured eight times, yielding 40 spectra from five biological observations; the technical replicates are presented to illustrate within-sample visual consistency. Associations between the intensities of 22 spectral peaks and 12 biochemical variables were explored using Pearson correlation.
RESULTS: Plasma biochemical parameters showed changes during the pre-competition tapering period, including decreases in CK and CRP and increases in glutathione and testosterone, whereas cortisol remained relatively stable. FTIR spectra exhibited consistent vibrational profiles with changes in selected band intensities over time. Linear regression identified strong associations between glutathione levels and FTIR bands at 671, 699, and 721 cm-1 (R 2 = 0.80-0.92), as well as between cortisol and the 3,009 cm-1 band (R 2 = 0.77). Because of the limited number of observations (n = 5), these findings are preliminary and require validation in larger cohorts.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated plasma measurements using ATR-FTIR demonstrated technical feasibility and visual consistency during a short pre-competition period in the studied athlete, while identifying potential spectral regions worthy of further investigation. The obtained results should be treated as preliminary. However, they do not provide evidence that ATR-FTIR enables the quantitative determination of glutathione or cortisol, or that it can be used to assess an athlete's competitive readiness. Confirmation of such capabilities requires studies involving adequately large and diverse groups of participants.

title: Adaptive Responses to "Top-up" Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia or Normoxia in Male University Basketball Players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Repeated-sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) has been shown to provide greater performance benefits than similar training in normoxia (RSN), whereas little is known regarding beneficial effects of RSH following a block of RSN. This study aimed to determine adaptive responses to "top-up" RSH.
METHODS: After pretesting, 15 male university basketball players completed 6 RSN sessions (2 sets of five to seven 6-second cycle sprints, 30-second intersprint, and 5-min interset recovery), followed by midtesting. Participants were then allocated to either hypoxic (HYP, n = 8) or normoxic (NOR, n = 7) group and completed 6 "top-up" sessions (3 sets of identical protocol), with 5 RSH (3000 m) plus 1 RSN in HYP and 6 RSN in NOR. Six-second and incremental cycle tests were performed to determine 1-second peak power (PP6s), 6-second mean power (MP6s), maximal aerobic power (MAP), and peak oxygen uptake (V˙O2peak) at pre, mid, and post. Repeated-sprint ability (PPRSA; averaged peak power over 10 sprints) was assessed during sessions 2, 6, and 12 in normoxia.
RESULTS: A 2-way mixed analysis of variance revealed main effects of time (P < .05, partial η2 = .349-.537) in all test variables (PP6s: Δ 10.6% [13.8%], MP6s: Δ 12.2% [13.6%], MAP: Δ 5.3% [4.3%], V˙O2peak: Δ 6.1% [5.5%]) without time-by-group interaction, whereas neither group improved PPRSA.
CONCLUSIONS: Twelve sessions of repeated-sprint training improved anaerobic and aerobic capacities in male basketball players, with no additional benefit of hypoxic exposure during the second training phase, suggesting increased training volume may have outweighed the environmental factor.

title: Osteoarthritis-Microenvironment-Triggered Phase Alteration of Injectable Conductive Hydrogel for Attenuating Cartilage Degradation.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is associated with excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which contributes substantially to chondrocyte dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cartilage degradation. Although stimuli-responsive hydrogels have emerged as promising platforms for OA therapy, conventional hydrogel-based systems exhibit limited sensitivity and require external detection equipment, highlighting the need for a simple, sensitive, and directly observable monitoring system. To address these challenges, we developed a ROS-triggered, in situ-forming gel-sol transition of a polydopamine (PDA)-loaded, diselenide-crosslinked polymer dot (PD) injectable hydrogel (HGC-PDA@PD or OA gel) as a monitorable theranostic for OA therapy at physiological temperature (37°C). The monitorable OA microenvironment-responsive hydrogel relied on interactions between the high ROS levels in OA cartilage and the OA gel, which triggered diselenide bond cleavage and the release of PDA from PD, causing a unique gel-sol transition of the OA gel. Owing to PDA release after diselenide breakage, the fluorescence and electroconductivity of the OA gel changed, which could serve as additional signals during OA detection. In vitro studies demonstrated the sensitive gel-sol transition of OA gel towards OA-induced immature articular chondrocytes (IL-1β/siSOD1/siCatalase-transfected iMACs). Furthermore, the OA gel showed a distinct gel-sol transition in cartilage of an in vivo OA mouse model compared with that in control mice. The lower transcription levels of cartilage matrix-degrading enzymes (ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, MMP-3, and MMP-13) observed after OA gel injection confirmed that the OA gel could scavenge ROS and attenuate cartilage damage, revealing its potential application for dual-function OA diagnosis and rehabilitation.

title: A TGF-β1-Binding and Stem Cell-Homing Peptide Hydrogel Loaded with BMSC-Exosomes Enhances the Endogenous Repair of Surgically Induced Osteochondral Defects.
abstract: To address the poor self-repair capacity of experimental osteochondral defects and the inefficacy of conventional hydrogels, this study developed a biodegradable peptide hydrogel, Exos@TRM. This study used an acute surgically created osteochondral defect model in rats, which does not fully reproduce experimental cartilage defects or chronic human cartilage degeneration. Based on the RADA16 framework, this hydrogel incorporates a TGF-β1-binding peptide and a stem cell-recruiting motif, and is loaded with exosomes derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). In vitro experiments demonstrated that Exos@TRM effectively binds TGF-β1, promotes BMSC migration, and enables sustained exosome release for up to one week, thereby facilitating BMSC proliferation and chondrogenic differentiation. In a rat cartilage defect model, Exos@TRM reduced pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages, recruited endogenous TGF-β1 and BMSCs to the injury site, promoted chondrogenic differentiation at week 3, and achieved tissue regeneration resembling natural cartilage with functional mechanical properties by week 8. Mechanistic studies confirmed that the regenerative effects are TGF-β1-dependent, and comprehensive biosafety evaluation revealed no systemic toxicity. This study demonstrates that Exos@TRM achieves significant cartilage repair without exogenous cells or high-dose growth factors through synergistic immunomodulation, localized TGF-β1 recruitment, and stem cell homing, offering a clinically promising strategy for experimental cartilage defects.

title: Limb Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in Rats is partially mediated by enhancing Necroptosis via Phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL.
abstract: Limb ischemia-reperfusion injury (L-IRI) causes severe skeletal muscle damage and functional impairment through activation of regulated cell-death and inflammatory pathways. Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrotic cell death mediated through the receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-RIPK3-mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) signaling axis. Prior experimental studies have shown that Necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) attenuates acute skeletal muscle ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. However, how Nec-1-sensitive protection relates to RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, circulating muscle injury markers, inflammatory responses, histological damage, and functional recovery during the early postischemic period remains incompletely defined. In this study, we used a rat model of unilateral hindlimb ischemia involving 3 hours of ischemia followed by reperfusion for up to 7 days to evaluate these interrelated responses. Nec-1 was administered before ischemia and after reperfusion. L-IRI resulted in elevated plasma creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels, severe histopathological injury, increased TUNEL staining, impaired grip strength, and reduced Modified Tarlov scores. These changes were accompanied by increased phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL, activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, and altered expression of injury-associated inflammatory mediators. Nec-1 treatment reduced RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, inflammatory mediator expression, circulating muscle injury markers, and histological injury while preserving muscle architecture and improving functional recovery. These findings support and extend previous evidence that Nec-1-sensitive necroptosis-associated signaling contributes to early skeletal muscle injury following L-IRI. Pharmacologic targeting of regulated necrotic and inflammatory pathways warrants further investigation as a potential adjunct strategy for limiting acute skeletal muscle injury after limb reperfusion.

title: Beware the Muscle: Silent Exercise-Induced Aminotransferase Elevation as a Diagnostic Pitfall in Hepatology and Pretreatment Screening-A Report of Two Cases.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In clinical hepatology practice, pretreatment liver enzyme screening plays a key role in making management decisions, such as initiation of antituberculosis therapy or surveillance of chronic hepatitis B. Unrecognized extrahepatic sources of aminotransferase elevations can lead to misdiagnosis, inappropriate treatment alteration, and unnecessary invasive or costly investigations.
CASE PRESENTATION: We present two cases of active young males who were undergoing liver biochemical testing for therapeutic decision-making for other underlying illnesses. Patient one was undergoing baseline liver enzyme testing prior to first-line antituberculosis treatment initiation while patient two was undergoing surveillance for e-antigen-negative hepatitis B infection. Both patients had asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations mimicking acute hepatocellular injury. There was a marked and disproportionate elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) relative to alanine aminotransferase (ALT), in the setting of otherwise normal cholestatic and synthetic parameters. Targeted history revealed heavy resistance weight training prior to testing. Measurement of serum creatine kinase (CK) confirmed exercise-induced muscle injury, demonstrating elevated CK concentrations that paralleled the AST trajectory. Cessation of strenuous training led to rapid normalization of aminotransferases and a decline in CK levels, without interruption of tuberculosis management or unwarranted antiviral initiation.
CONCLUSION: Clinically silent exertional muscle injury is an underappreciated mimicker of acute liver injury. In patients presenting with isolated or disproportionate AST elevation, confirming a myogenic enzyme source via CK quantification can prevent misdiagnosis, eliminate unnecessary liver-directed workup, and avoid inappropriate modification or initiation of essential pharmacotherapy.

title: Biomembrane-Camouflaged Stents: Promising Strategies for Advanced Coronary Interventions.
abstract: Coronary stent implantation remains a cornerstone therapy for coronary artery disease, yet current stent technologies continue to face limitations including acute and late thrombosis, delayed re-endothelialization, chronic inflammation, and in-stent restenosis. These complications largely arise from the nonphysiological interface between the implanted device and the injured vascular microenvironment. Biomembrane-camouflaged stents have recently emerged as a promising strategy to engineer biologically instructive blood-contacting surfaces by integrating natural or artificial membrane systems onto stent platforms. In this review, we summarize recent advances in three major biomembrane-based strategies for coronary stent functionalization: cell membrane-camouflaged stents, liposome-camouflaged stents, and exosome-camouflaged stents. Biomimetic cell membrane coatings retain native bioactive signals that collectively facilitate immune evasion, thromboresistance, and vascular healing. Liposome-based coatings are tunable artificial biomembrane reservoirs for the localized delivery of anticoagulants, anti-inflammatories, nitric oxide releasers, antiproliferatives, and gene therapies. Exosome-functionalized stents further enable bioactive intercellular communication by transferring endogenous regulatory cargos that modulate endothelial regeneration, macrophage polarization, smooth muscle cell phenotype, oxidative stress, and neointimal remodeling. We further discuss fabrication approaches, biological mechanisms, preclinical evidence, translational barriers, and future design principles for these platforms. Although challenges remain in coating durability, sterilization, long-term storage, manufacturing reproducibility, and clinical validation, biomembrane-camouflaged stents represent a compelling direction for next-generation coronary intervention by transforming conventional stents from passive mechanical scaffolds into active regulators of vascular repair.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: Lower limb interjoint coordination in maximal successful snatch attempts during competition: a vector coding comparison of elite and sub-elite weightlifters.
abstract: The snatch requires precise temporal coordination among multiple joints, yet technique is often assessed using individual-joint measures, which may not fully capture inter-joint coordination throughout the lift. We compared lower-limb inter-joint coordination and coordination-mode composition between elite and sub-elite weightlifters during competition snatch attempts. Successful 1RM attempts by ten elite and ten sub-elite 73-kg weightlifters were recorded using a dual-camera system. Three-dimensional kinematics provided sagittal-plane hip, knee, and ankle angles. Vector coding quantified coupling-angle trajectories and coordination-mode proportions for hip-knee, hip-ankle, and knee-ankle pairs across six time-normalised phases. Circular regression compared trajectories, PERMANOVA tested phase-specific mode composition, and coupling-angle mapping (CAM) characterised within-phase proximal-distal dominance. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. No between-group differences were found in coupling-angle trajectories across joint pairs or phases. However, knee-ankle mode composition differed during Transition (F = 3.389, p = 0.039) and Turnover under the barbell (F = 2.833, p = 0.048), but not in other phases or joint pairs. These findings suggest that performance-level differences are reflected in phase-dependent distal regulation and temporal reorganisation rather than overall coupling-trajectory patterns.

title: Shallow under load? Prevalence of acetabular morphologies and their association with sport exposure during skeletal maturation in professional female football players: a retrospective study using data from the PROFE cohort.
abstract: We aimed to report the prevalence of acetabular morphologies in professional female footballers and explore the association between these morphologies and sport exposure during the period of skeletal maturation. 100 professional female footballers (200 hips) were included. Athletes with a history of systemic disease were excluded. Questionnaires obtained information on previous sport frequencies and age of menarche. Participants reported the minimum hours of sport played weekly during three age categories/stages of growth: cartilaginous hypertrophy (8-10 years), skeletal growth (11-12 years), and closure of growth plates (13-16 years). Participants underwent a pelvic radiograph. The Wiberg-center edge angle classified hips with normal coverage, borderline dysplasia, dysplasia or pincer morphology. Logistic regression models explored the association between prevalence of acetabular morphologies and minimum of sport hours played weekly in different age groups. Interactions with age of menarche were explored. From 200 hips, 32% were classified as having borderline dysplasia, 9% had dysplasia, 1% had pincer morphology, and 58% had normal coverage. Athletes with a later age of menarche had higher odds of dysplasia with increasing sport exposure between 8-10 (OR [95%CI] = 1.23 [1.05-1.44]). p = 0.011) and 11-12 years (OR [95%CI] = 1.21 [1.06-1.38], p = 0.006) compared to those with an earlier age of menarche. Skeletal maturation might be an important period for the development of acetabular morphology in female footballers. Exposure to high‑load sport activity during skeletal maturation and age of menarche may contribute to the development of hip dysplasia in these athletes.

title: Metabolic Bone Health in Female Patients: Focus on Foot and Ankle.
abstract: Metabolic bone health is crucial for the overall well-being of female patients. Female athletes and young females are of particular interest, as their skeletal systems are still developing and are sensitive to the hormonal and physical stress of training and diet. Stress fractures occur with higher frequency in females with risk factors such as low bone mineral density (BMD). When low bone mineral density occurs along with menstrual irregularities and relative energy deficiency, it completes the female triad (23, 27, and 28). Any discussion of female BMD and metabolic bone health must include the female triad.

title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis.
abstract: Skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity that relies on adult stem cells known as satellite cells (SCs), which differentiate into myogenic progenitors to drive muscle repair. How varying energy availability alters myogenesis, however, remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that intermittent fasting (IF) in mice upregulates a myogenic gene program, including Myomixer, a muscle-specific fusogen that facilitates the merging of progenitor cells into myofibers. IF enhances the regeneration of injured muscles by expanding the SC population and promoting the proliferation and fusion of myogenic progenitors. These effects are absent in an SC-depletion model. We show that fasting-induced EDA2R-NIK signaling increases Myomixer expression and fusion in myoblasts. Notably, mice lacking EDA2R or NIK fail to respond to the myogenic effects of IF. Furthermore, our data suggest that mice with Duchenne muscular dystrophy also benefit from an IF regimen. Therefore, IF-induced regeneration holds potential for aiding recovery from muscle damage.

title: Evaluation of a four-herb Chinese medicine formula at different concentrations on muscle damage and inflammation in a rat model of DOMS.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) impairs exercise recovery, while current treatments remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) formulas may provide safe, multi-target interventions.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the dose-dependent protective effects of a four-herb Chinese medicine formulation (safflower, Chinese Angelica, peach kernel and myrrh) against DOMS in a rat model.
METHODS: Thirty-two male SPF SD rats were randomly allocated to control or low- (1696 mg/kg), medium- (3392 mg/kg), or high-dose (6784 mg/kg) groups. The formulation was administered orally for 11 days, with DOMS induced by exhaustive swimming on day 8. Serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-exercise.
RESULTS: The medium- and high-dose groups exhibited significantly lower serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 levels than controls, with the high-dose group showing the largest reductions. The low-dose group showed limited or no significant reductions in most markers, demonstrating a clear dose-dependent protective effect.
CONCLUSIONS: The formulation dose-dependently attenuates muscle damage and inflammation in a rat DOMS model, with high-dose treatment achieving the fastest recovery. Clinical trials are warranted to confirm the efficacy and safety in humans.

title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.
